en: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad, together with the commentary composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya:
the Śikṣā Chapter.
Salutation to that one whose nature is knowledge, from whom the entire world is born, into whom alone it is dissolved, and by whom this very world is sustained.
I perpetually bow down to those venerable teachers by whom all the Vedāntas were previously explained according to the standards of words, sentences, and means of valid cognition.
By the grace of my teacher, this commentary on the essence of the Taittirīyaka is being composed by me for those who desire its meaning to be clearly elucidated.

In the preceding section, the obligatory rites were taught for the purpose of exhausting accumulated sins, and the optional rites for those desiring specific fruits. Now, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is introduced for the purpose of abandoning the cause of the undertaking of karma. Desire (*kāma*) must be the cause of karma, because it is that which impels one to act. For those whose desires are fulfilled, in the absence of desire, there is no engagement in activity since they abide in their own Self. And when the Self is desired, there is the fulfillment of all desires. For the Self is indeed Brahman; the author will later state that the knower of That attains the Supreme.

Therefore, liberation is the effortless abiding in one's own self upon the cessation of ignorance; for the scriptures state: "He finds fearlessness and a firm foundation" (TaittU 2.7.1) and "He reaches this Self consisting of bliss" (TaittU 2.8.5), and so forth. Since there is no undertaking of optional or prohibited actions, and since commenced actions are exhausted through experience, and since there is an absence of transgression through the constant performance of obligatory duties, liberation is simply abiding in one's own self without effort.

Alternatively, if it is argued that liberation arises from karma alone because karma is the cause of that unsurpassed bliss denoted by the word "heaven" (*svarga*), we say no; for karma is manifold. Indeed, there exist many karmas performed in various previous births—some whose fruits have already begun to ripen and some whose fruits have not—which possess mutually contradictory results.

Therefore, since it is impossible for those [karmas] whose fruits have not yet begun to be exhausted through enjoyment in a single lifetime, the commencement of a new body caused by the remaining karma occurs, and the existence of residual karma is established. This is known from hundreds of scriptural and traditional texts such as, "Those here whose conduct was pleasant... (ChU 5.10.7), and "Then by the remainder... Furthermore, the claim that obligatory rites (*nitya*) are intended for the exhaustion of uncommenced desirable and undesirable fruits is incorrect, because scripture declares that there is transgression (*pratyavāya*) in their non-performance.

For the word *pratyavāya* refers to something undesirable; since it is accepted that obligatory rites (*nitya*) are for the purpose of avoiding the future *pratyavāya*—which consists of suffering and is caused by the non-performance of what is obligatory—they are not for the purpose of exhausting karma whose fruit has not yet begun. Even if obligatory rites were for the purpose of exhausting karma whose fruit has not yet begun, they would exhaust only impure [karma], not pure [karma], because there is no contradiction between them. Indeed, no contradiction with obligatory rites is possible in the case of karma that has a desired fruit, because such karma is of a pure nature.

For it is logical that there is a contradiction between the pure and the impure. Furthermore, since desires—which are the causes of karma—cannot be ceased in the absence of knowledge, the destruction of all karma is not possible [through mere non-performance]. For one who does not know the Self, desire exists because its objects are things other than the Self; moreover, desire for one's own Self is impossible because it is eternally attained. It has been stated that the Self is itself the Supreme Brahman. As for the non-performance of obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*), that is a mere absence; therefore, the arising of sin (*pratyavāya*) from such non-performance is untenable.

Therefore, since the non-performance of obligatory duties (*nitya*) is the defining characteristic of the transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from previously accumulated sins—as in the expression "one who does not perform the prescribed duty" (*akurvan vihitaṃ karma*, ViP 3.18.39)—the use of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is not untenable. Otherwise, the claim that "the arising of existence [occurs] from the absence of [existence]" would contradict all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, the notion that one remains established in one's own self without effort is untenable.

As for what was said—that because unsurpassed bliss, which is denoted by the word "heaven," is caused by ritual action (*karman*), liberation (*mokṣa*) must therefore originate from action alone—that is not so, because liberation is eternal. For nothing that is eternal is ever produced in the world; whatever is produced is impermanent. Therefore, liberation is not something originated by action. If it is argued that actions accompanied by knowledge (*vidyā*) have the capacity to produce an eternal result, we say no, because of contradiction. It is a contradiction to say that something is both eternal and produced.

If it is argued that liberation is indeed "begun" (attained) even though it is eternal—just like the non-existence following destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva)—on the grounds that whatever has perished does not arise again, we say no; for liberation is of the nature of a positive entity (bhāva). It is impossible for even the non-existence following destruction to be "begun," because since non-existence lacks any specific qualities, this [assertion] is a mere conceptual fiction. For non-existence is defined as the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) of existence.

For just as an entity, though itself undifferentiated, is distinguished by things such as jars and cloths—such that there is the "undifferentiated jar-entity" and the "undifferentiated cloth-entity"—so too, although non-existence (*abhāva*) is devoid of distinctions, it is conceptualized through its association with actions and qualities, just like substances and so forth. For non-existence does not coexist with qualifiers in the same way that a lotus or similar object does; if it possessed qualifiers, it would simply be an existence (*bhāva*). If it is argued that because the agent of knowledge and action is eternal, liberation—which is produced by the continuum of knowledge and action—is also eternal, we say no.

Because agency is of the nature of suffering, like the flow of the Gaṅgā, and because liberation would be impossible if agency were not brought to rest; therefore, since liberation is abiding in one's own self upon the cessation of the causes of appropriation—namely ignorance, desire, and action—the Upaniṣad is commenced for the purpose of the knowledge of Brahman, wherein the Self itself is Brahman, and through the realization of that, ignorance is removed.

"Upaniṣad" refers to knowledge (*vidyā*). It is so called because it shatters or destroys the darkness of embryonic existence, birth, old age, and so forth for those who practice it; or because it brings one to the realization of Brahman; or because the supreme good is seated (*upaniṣanna*) within it. Since the book has that as its purpose, the text itself is also called "Upaniṣad."

Oṃ! May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Salutation to Brahman! Salutation to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Satya. May that protect me; may that protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker. Oṃ! Peace! Peace! Peace!
Thus ends the first section in the chapter on training.

May Mitra—the deity presiding over the function of the prāṇa (out-breath) and the day—be auspicious (*śam*) for us. Likewise, may Varuṇa—the deity presiding over the function of the apāna (in-breath) and the night—be so. May Aryaman, who presides over the eye and the sun; Indra, over strength; Bṛhaspati, over speech and the intellect; and Viṣṇu of the wide stride (*urukrama*), who presides over the feet—may they all be auspicious for us. Thus are the deities of the internal self (*adhyātma*); the phrase "may they be auspicious for us" is to be supplied everywhere.

For since those [winds] bring about happiness by not obstructing the acquisition, retention, and application of knowledge, their status as the agents of that happiness is prayed for with the words, "May they be auspicious to us. By one who desires to know the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the acts of salutation and the recitation of the *Brahma-vidyā* are performed with respect to Vāyu for the sake of pacifying obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman. Since the fruits of all actions depend upon Him, Vāyu is Brahman; "to that Brahman, obeisance" (*namaḥ*)—the ellipsis of the sentence being "I perform an act of prostration."

"Salutations to you, O Vāyu! I pay homage"—by these words, both in the indirect and the direct sense, Vāyu alone is being addressed. Furthermore, since you alone, in relation to the eyes and other senses, are the external, proximate, unobstructed, and manifest Brahman, therefore I shall speak of you alone as the manifest Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as the *ṛta*—the matter well-determined in the intellect according to the scriptures and according to what ought to be done—because that is dependent upon you.

"Truth" (*satyam*) is that very [principle] which is accomplished through speech and body; since even that is accomplished only by depending upon you, I shall speak of you alone as Truth. May that Brahman, called Vāyu, who consists of all this and has been thus praised by me, protect me by bestowing knowledge upon those seeking knowledge. May that same Brahman protect the teacher, the speaker, by bestowing the capacity for speaking. The repetition—"May he protect me, may he protect the speaker"—is for the sake of showing reverence.
"Oṃ, peace! Peace! Peace!"—this threefold utterance is for the purpose of pacifying the obstacles encountered in the acquisition of knowledge, whether they be internal, external, or celestial.
Thus ends the first section (anu-vāka). // 1 //
Oṃ. We shall explain phonetics (śīkṣā). [It consists of] letter, accent, measure, strength, melody, and continuity. Thus has been stated the chapter on phonetics. This is the second recitation.

Since the Upaniṣads have as their primary purpose the knowledge of the meaning [of the Veda], lest there be a cessation of effort in the recitation of the texts, the Śīkṣādhyāya is commenced. *Śikṣā* means that by which one is taught (*śikṣyate*), characterized by the correct pronunciation of phonemes and so forth; or, *śikṣā* refers to the phonemes and so forth themselves, as they are what are to be learned (*śikṣyante*). *Śīkṣā* is simply *śikṣā*; the lengthening of the vowel is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). We shall explain that *śīkṣā*, that is, we shall clearly and completely expound it. This form is derived from the root *cakṣiṅ*, which is replaced by *khyāñ* and preceded by the prefix *vyāṅ*, because the object of the action is made manifest (*vyakta*).

In this context, *varṇa* refers to the phonemes beginning with *a*; *svara* refers to the accents such as the acute (*udātta*); *mātrā* refers to the durations such as the short (*hrasva*); *bala* refers to a specific degree of articulatory effort (*prayatna*); *sāman* refers to the evenness of pronunciation by avoiding extremes among the phonemes; and *santāna* refers to continuity, meaning *saṃhitā*. This chapter, in which this subject matter to be learned (*śikṣitavya*) is taught—that is, the science of phonetics (*śikṣā*)—is thus called the "Chapter on Phonetics" (*śīkṣādhyāya*). The word "spoken" (*ukta*) serves as a concluding statement.
Thus ends the second section (anuvāka). // 2 //

May our fame be shared; may our spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) be shared. Now, therefore, we shall explain the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the *Saṃhitā* with respect to five topics: concerning the worlds (*adhiloka*), concerning the luminaries (*adhijyautiṣa*), concerning knowledge (*adhividyā*), concerning progeny (*adhipraja*), and concerning the self (*adhyātma*). These they call the "Great *Saṃhitās*. Now, concerning the worlds: the earth is the prior form; the sky is the posterior form; space is the junction.

Now the *Saṃhitopaniṣad* is being stated. Regarding that, whatever fame is obtained as a result of the thorough knowledge of the *Saṃhitopaniṣad* and so forth, may that belong to both of us—the disciple and the teacher—jointly. And may the splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) and luster (*tejas*) resulting from that also belong to us jointly; such is the benediction (*āśis*) expressed by the disciple. For a request is appropriate for the disciple because he has not yet achieved his goal, but not for the teacher, since he has already achieved his goal. Indeed, it is the teacher who is called one who has achieved his purpose (*kṛtārtha*).

Now, immediately following the preceding section on the rules for the characteristics of the *adhyāya*, because the intellect—having been thoroughly cultivated by the text—is not able to be suddenly introduced to the subject of understanding the meaning, we shall therefore explain the *upaniṣad* of the *saṃhitā*; that is, the philosophical vision (*darśana*) concerning the *saṃhitā*. This will be explained in close connection with the text itself, within five topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), which serve as the bases or subjects of knowledge.

"What are they? he asks. He says: "That which is the vision regarding the worlds (*adhiloka*)—that is, regarding the various worlds—is *adhiloka*. Likewise, there is *adhijyautiṣa*, *adhividyā*, *adhipraja*, and *adhyātma*. These five subjects of the Upaniṣads, because they have the great entities beginning with the worlds as their object and because they have the *Saṃhitā* as their object, are called and spoken of by those who know the Veda as the "Great *Saṃhitās*" (*mahāsaṃhitā*). Now, among those [five] presented here, the vision regarding the worlds (*adhiloka*) is being stated.

The word "atha" (then) is used everywhere for the purpose of indicating the sequence of the meditations. "Earth" is the *pūrvarūpa* (prior form); *pūrvarūpa* means the prior letter. What is meant is that one should perform the meditation on earth upon the prior letter of a *saṃhitā* (continuous text). Likewise, "heaven" is the *uttararūpa* (subsequent form), and "space" is the intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*). "The junction" (*sandhi*) is the middle between the prior and subsequent forms; it is so called because the prior and subsequent forms are joined together in it.

"Wind is the connection"—thus with respect to the worlds. Now with respect to the luminaries: fire is the prior form; the sun is the subsequent form; the waters are the junction; lightning is the connection—thus with respect to the luminaries. Now with respect to knowledge: the teacher is the prior form.

The pupil is the subsequent form; knowledge is the junction; the teaching is the connection. This is with respect to knowledge (*adhividyam*). Now, with respect to progeny (*adhiprajam*): the mother is the prior form; the father is the subsequent form; offspring is the junction; procreation is the connection. This is with respect to progeny.

Now, with respect to the self: the lower jaw is the prior form; the upper jaw is the subsequent form; speech is the junction; and the tongue is the connection. This is with respect to the self. These, then, are the Great Connections. Whoever knows these Great Connections as thus explained becomes united with offspring, with cattle, with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*), with food, and with the heavenly world.
Thus ends the third section.

"Vāyu is the connection (*sandhāna*); it is called a connection because by means of it things are connected. Thus has been stated the teaching concerning the world (*adhiloka*). Now follows the teaching concerning the luminaries (*adhijyautiṣa*), and so forth, which is the same as before. "These [connections]"—thus what has been said is now demonstrated. Whoever thus meditates upon these explained great connections (*mahāsaṃhitā*) "knowing" (*veda*) them—here "knowing" signifies meditation (*upāsana*), because the context concerns knowledge (*vijñāna*), and because of the statement: "O Prācīnayogya, meditate! (TaittU 1.6.2).

And meditation (*upāsana*), according to the scriptures, is a continuous flow of identical cognitions, unmixed with other cognitions, and having as its object the focal point prescribed by the scriptures. Furthermore, the meaning of the word "meditation" is well-known in common usage, as in the expressions "he meditates on his teacher" (*gurum upāste*) or "he meditates on the king" (*rājānam upāste*). For one who attends constantly upon his teachers and others is said to "meditate," and he obtains the fruit of that meditation. Therefore, here too, he who knows thus is joined with offspring and so forth, ending with heaven;
the meaning is that he attains the fruits such as offspring.
Thus ends the third section.

He who is the bull of the meters, possessing all forms, who was born from the nectar of the meters—may he, Indra, strengthen me with wisdom. O God, may I become a bearer of the nectar of immortality. May my body be radiant; may my tongue be most sweet; may I hear much with my two ears. You are the treasury of sacred knowledge (*brahman*), covered by wisdom. Protect what I have heard.

Bringing, spreading out, and quickly preparing for herself garments, cattle, food, and drink for me at all times—therefore, bring prosperity to me, together with woolly livestock; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) come hither; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge go forth; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge be disciplined; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge be self-controlled; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge be tranquil; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge be peaceful; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge be utterly calm; *svāhā*.

May I be glorious among the people, svāhā! May I be better than the wealthy, svāhā! O Bhaga, may I enter into you, svāhā! O Bhaga, enter into me, svāhā! In you, who have a thousand branches, O Bhaga, I cleanse myself, svāhā! Just as waters flow down a slope, just as the months follow the revolving year, so may the students of sacred knowledge come to me from every side, O Dhātṛ, svāhā! You are my neighbor; shine upon me, come to me!
Thus ends the fourth section.

The passages beginning with "He who [is the bull] of the *chandasaḥ*" are stated as the means for attaining wisdom (*medhā*) and prosperity (*śrī*) for one who desires them; this is because of the indicative marks seen in the texts: "May he, being Indra, quicken me with wisdom" (TaittU 1.4.1) and "From that, bring me prosperity" (TaittU 1.4.2). He who is the "bull" (*ṛṣabha*)—like a bull among the *chandasaḥ*, i.e., the Vedas—due to his preeminence. He is "multiform" (*viśvarūpa*), possessing all forms, according to another scriptural passage beginning with "Just as by a peg... (ChU 2.23.3). For this very reason, the syllable *oṃ* possesses the nature of a bull.

Since the syllable *oṃ* is indeed the object of worship here, its praise through words such as "bull" (*ṛṣabha*) and so forth is entirely appropriate. From the *chandāṃsi*, that is, from the Vedas—for the Vedas are indeed immortality—from that immortality he was born. The meaning is that for Prajāpati, who was performing austerity and desired to grasp the most excellent essence from the worlds, the gods, the Vedas, and the *vyāhṛtis*, the syllable *oṃ* appeared as that most excellent essence. For the production of the eternal *oṃ* cannot be conceived in a literal sense.

May that very *oṃkāra*, who is Indra, the Lord of all desires, the Supreme Lord, satisfy (*spṛṇotu*)—that is, gladden or strengthen—me with wisdom (*medhayā*), that is, with discernment (*prajñayā*). For it is the power of discernment that is sought; for the knowledge of Brahman, which is the cause of immortality (*amṛta*), is the subject at hand. O God, may I become a "holder" (*dhāraṇaḥ*), one who possesses [this knowledge]. Furthermore, may my body be "far-seeing" (*vicarṣaṇam*), meaning far-sighted and fit [for this purpose]. The word "may it be" (*bhūyāt*) is understood as a modification of the third person [to the first person].

"May my tongue be most honeyed"—that is to say, exceedingly sweet in speech. "With both ears, may I hear much"—that is to say, may I become a great listener. The meaning of the sentence is: "May my aggregate of body and organs be fit for the knowledge of the Self. Indeed, it is for that very purpose that wisdom (*medhā*) is prayed for. You are the sheath of Brahman, the Supreme Self; for, like a sword, you are the locus of its perception.

For you are the emblem (*pratīka*) of Brahman; in you, Brahman is perceived. "Covered by wisdom" means concealed by worldly intelligence (*laukikaprajñā*); the sense is that your true nature is unknown to those of ordinary intellect. "Protect my *śruta*"—that is, the knowledge of the Self and so forth, preceded by hearing (*śravaṇa*)—means: perform its attainment, its non-forgetting, and so on. These mantras are for the purpose of recitation (*japa*) by one who desires wisdom. (TaittUBh 1.4.1)

Now, the mantras for one desiring prosperity (śrī) for the purpose of the fire-sacrifice (homa) are being stated: "Bringing" means leading near; "spreading" means extending, because that is the function of the root *tan* (to extend); "performing" means accomplishing. "Without delay" (*aciram*) means very quickly; the lengthening of the vowel is Vedic (chāndasa). Or [it may mean] "for a long time. What does he say? "Clothes" (*vāsāṃsi*), meaning garments, and "cows" (*gāvaḥ*), meaning cattle—these are for me.

"Bring forth that Fortune which always makes food and drink its primary concern; bring it from the production of intelligence (*medhā*), for the fortune of one lacking intelligence leads only to misfortune. Of what kind? Bring it that is 'hairy,' endowed with goats, sheep, and other livestock, and joined with other animals. By virtue of the context, the syllable *Oṃ* alone is connected [to this]. *Svāhā*: the utterance *svāhā* is for the purpose of indicating the end of the mantra used for the oblation (*homa*). "May they come to me."

The phrase "may they come to me" is connected with what follows: "the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins). [It continues: "may they measure out for me, may they measure forth for me, may they subdue for me, may they pacify for me," and so on. "May I be glorious"—that is, may I be possessed of glory among the people, among the assembly of men. "May I be better than the wealthy"—the meaning is: may I be more excellent, more praiseworthy, and distinguished from those of the same class; that is, may I be superior to a person of my own kind who is merely wealthy. May I be distinguished from one who is even more opulent. This is the sense.

Furthermore: "O Blessed One, worthy of worship, I shall enter you, who are the sheath of Brahman; having entered, I shall become non-different from you, meaning that I shall become your very self. And you too, O Blessed One, worthy of worship, enter me; let there be oneness between us alone. In you, who have a thousand branches and many divisions, I wipe away—purify—my sinful deed. Just as in the world waters flow along a *pravat*, that is, along a downward-sloping or low-lying place.

And just as the months are the "day-decayers" (*ahar-jaraḥ*) and the year is the "day-decayer"—meaning that by revolving through the days it causes the worlds to decay, or that the days themselves decay and are contained within it—so too, O Creator (*dhātar*), O Ordainer of all, may the students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*) come to me from all sides, from every direction. A "neighbor" (*prativeśaḥ*) is a place for removing fatigue, meaning a nearby house; such a neighbor art thou.

Like a neighbor, you are the place for those of virtuous conduct to remove all sins and sufferings; therefore, shine upon me, reveal yourself to me, and take refuge in me. The meaning is: "Make me consist of you and have me as your very self, like iron permeated by mercury. In this section concerning knowledge (*vidyā*), that which is mentioned as the desire for prosperity (*śrī*) has wealth as its purpose; wealth is for the sake of ritual action (*karman*); and ritual action is for the sake of destroying accumulated demerit (*durita*). For when that is destroyed, knowledge shines forth.
And so says the Smṛti: "Knowledge arises for men from the destruction of sinful karma; they behold the Self within themselves, as if in the surface of a clear mirror" (Mahābhārata 12.197.8).
Thus ends the fourth section (anuvāka). 4.

"Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ"—these indeed are the three vyāhṛtis. Of these, Māhācamasya used to proclaim this fourth one: "Mahaḥ. That is Brahman; that is the Self (ātman); the other deities are its limbs. "Bhūḥ" is indeed this world; "bhuvaḥ" is the intermediate space; "suvaḥ" is yonder world.

“Maha” is the sun; indeed, by the sun all the worlds are magnified. “Bhūḥ” is Agni; “bhuvaḥ” is Vāyu; “suvaḥ” is the sun; “maha” is the moon; indeed, by the moon all the luminaries are magnified. “Bhūḥ” is the Ṛg verses; “bhuvaḥ” is the Sāman chants; “suvaḥ” is the Yajus formulas.

“Maha” is Brahman; indeed, by means of Brahman all the Vedas are magnified. “Bhūḥ” is indeed the out-breath (prāṇa); “Bhuvaḥ” is the in-breath (apāna); “Suvaḥ” is the diffused breath (vyāna); “Maha” is food; indeed, by means of food all the vital breaths are magnified. These four [syllables] are each fourfold; thus there are four sets of four sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis). He who knows them knows Brahman; all the gods bring him tribute.
Thus ends the fifth section.

The meditation concerning the *saṃhitā* has been stated; following that, the mantras for one desiring intelligence and one desiring prosperity have been set forth, and these too are intended solely for the application of knowledge through a traditional succession. Immediately thereafter, the meditation upon Brahman as consisting of the *vyāhṛtis*, which has self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) as its fruit, is introduced. "Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ"—the word "iti" (thus) is for the purpose of indicating what has been stated, and "etās tisraḥ" (these three) is for the purpose of referring back to those already indicated. Those referred back are recalled by the phrase "vai" (indeed).

These three *vyāhṛtis* are traditionally remembered as well-known; this is the fourth *vyāhṛti* among them, which he utters. Māhācamasya—the offspring of Mahācamasa—proclaims this fourth one. The particle *u ha sma* is used here for the purpose of recounting a past event, meaning that he knew or perceived it. The mention of Māhācamasya is for the sake of remembering the seer (*ṛṣi*). It is understood from the instruction given here that the remembrance of the seer is also an auxiliary element of the meditation (*upāsanā*).

This *vyāhṛti* which is "Maha" according to the tradition of Māhācamasya—that is Brahman, for Brahman is great (*mahat*) and the *vyāhṛti* is "Maha. But what is that? It is the Self (*ātman*). It is the Self because of the root *āp*, meaning "to pervade. And the other *vyāhṛtis*—the worlds, the gods, the Vedas, and the vital breaths—are pervaded by this *vyāhṛti*-Self, which consists of the sun, the moon, Brahman, and food. Therefore, the other deities are its limbs or members. The mention of "deities" is intended as an illustration for the worlds and the rest.

Since all things, beginning with the world of the gods, are constituent parts of this *vyāhṛti* which is *mahat*, he therefore says: "By means of the sun and so forth, the worlds and the rest are magnified (*mahīyante*). For the limbs of a self are magnified; "magnifying" (*mahana*) means growth or increase. Thus, the meaning is that they "are magnified," i.e., they grow. This world, fire, the *Ṛgveda*, and the out-breath (*prāṇa*) constitute the first *vyāhṛti*, "bhūḥ. The intermediate space, wind, the *Sāmaveda*, and the diffused breath (*apāna*) constitute the second *vyāhṛti*, "bhuvaḥ."

"That world" is the sun, "the sacrificial formulas" are the diffused breath (*vyāna*); this is the third *vyāhṛti*, *suvaḥ*. "The sun" is the moon, "the priest" is food; this is the fourth *vyāhṛti*, *mahaḥ*. In this manner, each successive [set] consists of four parts.

"Mahas" is Brahman; "Brahman" is the syllable *oṃ*, because in the context of sound, nothing else is possible. The rest has already been explained. "These indeed are four, and [each] fourth"—these indeed are the four, namely *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *suvar*, and *mahas*; each one is fourfold, meaning they consist of four kinds. The word *dhā* expresses the sense of "kind. The meaning is that being four each, they become fourfold. The repetition of these as they have been defined is for the purpose of restricting their meditation exactly in that manner.

He who knows those aforementioned *vyāhṛtis* knows—that is, understands—that Brahman. What is that Brahman? [Objection: But surely, when it has been known that "That Brahman is the Self," one need not say "he knows Brahman" as if he were ignorant. [Reply: No! There is no fault here, because there is a desire to state its specific qualities. It is true that Brahman, the Self, has been known through the fourth *vyāhṛti*; however, its specific qualities—such as being perceivable within the heart and consisting of mind (*manomaya*)—have not yet been stated.

The collection of attributes in the form of qualifiers and the qualified, ending with "abounding in peace" (*śāntisamṛddham*), is thus understood. Desiring to explain that, the scripture—as if considering Brahman to be unknown—says, "he knows Brahman. Therefore, there is no fault. For the intention is this: he who knows Brahman as distinguished by the collection of attributes about to be described, he knows Brahman. Consequently, this [verse] forms a single syntactical unit with the subsequent section, for the meditation (*upāsana*) is one in both sections; this is also evident from the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) beginning with "By *bhūḥ* he becomes established in Agni" points to the unity of the meditation; furthermore, there is an absence of an injunction [for separate meditations]. Indeed, there is no word that serves as an injunction such as "the Veda is to be meditated upon. And the phrase "he who knows this" (*yo veda*) in the section on the *vyāhṛtis* does not differentiate the meditations, because its meaning will be explained later. That it has a meaning to be explained later was stated by the words "because of the desire to express its specific details," and so forth. The meaning is: "All the gods bring—that is, they convey—the *bālī* (offering) to this very person who knows, once his self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) has been attained."
Thus ends the fifth section.

It has been stated that the other deities are limbs of the Brahman whose nature consists of the vyāhṛtis *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*, and *mahaḥ*. For the sake of the direct perception and the meditation upon this very Brahman of which they are the limbs, the space within the heart is declared to be its location, just as Śālagrāma is for Viṣṇu. For when that Brahman is meditated upon there—distinguished by attributes such as consisting of mind—it is directly perceived, like an amalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand. Furthermore, the path for attaining the state of being the Self of all must be explained; thus, the next section (anuvāka) begins.

That which is this space within the heart—in it is this person consisting of mind, immortal and golden. Between the two palates is that which hangs down like a nipple; that is the source of Indra. Where the parting of the hair occurs, having parted the two skull-halves, [the breath] establishes itself in fire with "Bhūḥ," and in wind with "Bhuvaḥ."

The word "he" (saḥ), having been displaced, is connected with the phrase "this person" (ayaṃ puruṣaḥ). "Within the heart" means inside the heart. The "heart" is a mass of flesh shaped like a lotus, the abode of the vital breaths (prāṇas), containing many tubular channels (nāḍīs), with its stalk pointing upward and its opening downward; it is well known and observed when an animal is being dissected. Within that [heart] is this space (ākāśa), which is well known just like the space within a water-pot (karaka). In that [space] is this person.

He is called *puruṣa* because he has filled (*pūrita*) the city (*puri*), or because he has filled the worlds beginning with the earth; he is "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*). "Mind" (*manas*) means consciousness (*vijñāna*). He is "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*) because he is perceived through it, as it is the instrument of the act of knowing (*manute*). Alternatively, "mind" is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) by which one thinks; he is "consisting of that" because he identifies with it, or because it is his characteristic mark. He is "immortal" (*amṛta*), meaning his nature is not subject to death; he is "golden" (*hiraṇmaya*), meaning he consists of light.

For that wise one who has thus directly realized this very characteristic within the space of the heart and has become one with the Self, the path for attaining the state of the Lord is now described. The channel named Suṣumnā, which extends upward from the heart, is well-known in the Yoga scriptures; it goes between the two well-known palates in the middle. And "between" refers to the interior of that piece of flesh which hangs down like a breast in the middle of the two palates.

And where the "end of the hair" (keśānta)—the end, limit, or root of the hair—is "turned," meaning it exists as a distinct region on the crown of the head; having reached that place, [the vein] has emerged there. Having "pushed aside," meaning having divided and split open the two skull-halves (śīrṣakapāle), she has gone forth. This is the "womb of Indra" (sendrayoni)—the womb or path of Indra, who is Brahman; the meaning is that it is the gateway for attaining one's true nature.

Thus, the knower who perceives the self as consisting of mind, having departed through the crown of the head, becomes established in that fire which is the presiding deity of this world, which consists of the *vyāhṛti* "Bhūḥ," and which is a limb of the Great Brahman; the meaning is that he pervades this world by means of the nature of fire. Likewise, he is established in the wind, which is the essence of the second *vyāhṛti*, "Bhuvaḥ"; the phrase "he is established" is understood to carry over.

"Suvaḥ" is in the sun; "mahaḥ" is in Brahman. One attains self-sovereignty; one attains the Lord of the Mind. He becomes the Lord of Speech, the Lord of Sight, the Master of Hearing, and the Lord of Discernment. From that, he becomes this: Brahman, whose body is space, whose self is truth, who delights in vital breath, whose bliss is the mind, who is perfected in peace, and who is immortal. Thus, O Prācīnayogya, do thou worship.
Thus ends the sixth section.

In "Svaḥ," he is established in the Sun, which is the essence of the third *vyāhṛti*; in "Mahaḥ," he is established in Brahman, which is the essence of the fourth *vyāhṛti* and the whole. Having remained within them as their very self, having become Brahman, he attains self-sovereignty—the state of being a self-ruler; he himself becomes a king and sovereign, just as Brahman is to the gods who constitute its limbs. And all the gods, as its limbs, bring tribute to him, just as they do to Brahman. He attains the Lord of the Mind (*manasaspati*).

For he is the lord of all minds because Brahman is the self of all; indeed, by means of all minds, he thinks that [Brahman], and thus the knower attains it. Furthermore, he becomes the lord of all speech; likewise, he is the lord of eyes, the lord of ears, and the lord of cognitions. Because he is the self of all, the meaning is that he comes to possess those [faculties] through the instruments of all living beings.

Moreover, this is even more than that. What is it? It is said: "having space for its body" (*ākāśa-śarīra*). Its body is space, or its body is as subtle as space; thus it is "having space for its body. What is that? It is the Brahman under discussion. "Having truth for its self" (*satyātman*): truth is its form—whether manifest or unmanifest, non-false, or its own essential nature—and its very nature (*ātman*) is that; thus it is "having truth for its self. "Delighting in the vital breaths" (*prāṇārāma*): that whose play and sport (*āramaṇa*) is among the vital breaths is "delighting in the vital breaths."

That in which the vital breaths find their delight is "the delight of the vital breaths" (*prāṇārāma*). That whose mind is bliss is "the bliss of the mind" (*manonanda*); that is, the mind which consists of bliss and produces happiness alone. "Abounding in peace" (*śāntisamṛddha*): peace (*śānti*) means tranquility (*upaśama*). It is "abounding in peace" because it is enriched by peace, or because it is perceived as being enriched by peace. "Immortal" (*amṛta*) means having the nature of non-death. This further qualification is to be understood as applying specifically to that [Self] described previously as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth.

Thus, the words of the teacher—"O Prācīnayogya, meditate upon Brahman as characterized by the qualities of consisting of mind and so forth, as previously described"—are spoken for the sake of showing reverence.
Thus ends the sixth section.

That Brahman consisting of the *vyāhṛtis* which was previously mentioned as the object of meditation is now described in terms of its nature as the fivefold (*pāṅkta*) aggregate beginning with the earth. Because of its association with the number five, it attains the character of the *paṅkti* metre; consequently, everything possesses this fivefold nature. Furthermore, the sacrifice is fivefold, according to the Vedic revelation: "The *paṅkti* consists of five feet; the sacrifice is fivefold" (AiB 5.24.1). Therefore, when one conceives of everything—from the worlds down to the self—as fivefold, one is conceiving of the sacrifice itself.
By means of that sacrifice thus conceived, one attains Prajāpati, who consists of the fivefold. To the question, "In what way is all this fivefold? he says:

The earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the quarters, and the intermediate directions; fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the stars; the waters, the plants, the trees, space, and the self—this is with reference to the objective world (*adhibhūta*). Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*): the out-breath, the diffused breath, the in-breath, the upward breath, and the equalizing breath; the eye, the ear, the mind, speech, and the skin; the skin, the flesh, the sinews, the bone, and the marrow. Having analyzed this, the Seer said: "All this is fivefold; by means of the fivefold, one attains the fivefold."
Thus ends the seventh section.

"Earth, intermediate space, heaven, the quarters, and the intermediate quarters"—this is the pentad of the worlds (*lokapāṅktam*). "Fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the stars"—this is the pentad of the deities (*devatāpāṅktam*). "Water, herbs, trees, space, and the self"—this is the pentad of the elements (*bhūtapāṅktam*). The term "self" refers to the *virāj*, because of its governing role over the elements. This [phrase] "thus with respect to the elements" (*ity adhibhūtam*) is intended to indicate the two pentads of the worlds and the deities, since both the pentads of the worlds and the deities have already been mentioned.

Immediately thereafter, the three pentads pertaining to the internal self (*adhyātma*) are described: the pentad of vital airs beginning with *prāṇa*; the pentad of sense organs beginning with the eye; and the pentad of elements beginning with the skin. For all this internal [reality] consists of these. And the external is likewise a pentad. Having thus analyzed and conceptualized this, a seer (*ṛṣi*)—one endowed with such vision or someone else—spoke, that is, declared: "This."

What does he say?—"All this is indeed fivefold (pāṅkta). By means of the internal fivefold [nature], through the commonality of number, one strengthens, supports, and fulfills the external fivefold [world]. That is to say, it is perceived as having a single essence. The meaning is that he who knows "all this is thus fivefold" becomes the very self of Prajāpati. (TaittUBh 1.7.1)
Thus ends the seventh section.

"Om" is Brahman. "Om" is this entire universe. Indeed, "Om" is an imitation; for even when they say, "Make it heard," they cause it to be heard with "Om. They sing the Sāmans with "Om. They recite the Śastras with "Oṃ-śom. The Adhvaryu priest responds with the *pratigara* chant with "Om. The Brahmā priest gives his impulse with "Om. One authorizes the Agnihotra sacrifice with "Om. A Brāhmaṇa, about to speak, says, "May I attain Brahman," and he indeed attains Brahman.
Thus ends the eighth section.

The meditation upon Brahman as the *vyāhṛtis* has been taught; immediately following that, the meditation upon that very same Brahman in the form of the fivefold sacrifice (*pāṅkta*) was taught. Now, the meditation upon the syllable *Oṃ*, which serves as a limb for all meditations, is intended to be prescribed. For when the syllable *Oṃ* is meditated upon through the vision of the higher and lower Brahman, even as a mere sound, it becomes a means for attaining the higher and lower Brahman. Indeed, it is the support for both the higher and lower Brahman, just as an image is for Viṣṇu.

"By this very means, one follows after one or the other," according to the Śruti (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.2). "Om. The word *iti* is for the purpose of delimiting the essential form. One should hold in the mind and meditate upon this syllable-form "Om" as Brahman; for everything here is of the nature of sound, and all is pervaded by the syllable Om. This is known from another Śruti passage: "As by a peg... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.3). Since that which is denoted is dependent upon its designator, all this is said to be the syllable Om.

The subsequent text is for the purpose of praising the syllable *oṃ*, because it is the object of meditation. "Om"—this is an imitation (*anukṛti*), that is, a mimicry. When another person says, "I shall do it" or "I shall go," having already done so or spoken thus, he mimics it by saying "Om. Therefore, the syllable *oṃ* is an imitation. The particles *ha*, *sma*, and *vai* indicate well-known facts; for the status of the syllable *oṃ* as an imitation is indeed well known. Furthermore, they cause the announcement to be made and respond to it after first giving the command, "Oṃ! Make it heard! Likewise, the singers of the Sāman chant the Sāmans, saying "Om."

"Oṃ śom"—thus do those who recite the *śastra* hymns pronounce them; likewise, the *adhvaryu* priest utters the response "oṃ. "Oṃ"—with this the *brahman* priest gives his impulse and permission. "Oṃ"—with this he gives permission for the *agnihotra*. When it is said, "I sacrifice," he grants permission with "oṃ" alone. "Oṃ"—when a *brāhmaṇa* is about to speak, that is, when he is about to perform a recitation (*pravacana*) or is about to study, he says "oṃ" and begins with "oṃ"; the meaning is that he begins in order to study.

Thinking, "May I attain Brahman," "May I reach it," or "I shall grasp it," one indeed attains Brahman. Alternatively, thinking, "May I attain Brahman," that is, the Supreme Self (paramātman), one who intends to declare or lead oneself [to it] says simply "Om. And by means of that syllable Om, he indeed attains Brahman. Since actions preceded by the syllable Om possess fruitfulness, therefore the meaning of the sentence is: "One should meditate upon the syllable Om as Brahman."
Thus ends the eighth section.

Righteousness and the study and teaching of the Vedas; truth and the study and teaching of the Vedas; austerity and the study and teaching of the Vedas; self-restraint and the study and teaching of the Vedas; tranquility and the study and teaching of the Vedas; the sacred fires and the study and teaching of the Vedas; the fire-sacrifice and the study and teaching of the Vedas; guests and the study and teaching of the Vedas; human duties and the study and teaching of the Vedas; and progeny and the study and teaching of the Vedas.

"Procreation and the study and teaching of the Veda," says Satyavacas Rāthītara. "Offspring and the study and teaching of the Veda," says Taponitya Pauruśiṣṭi. "Only the study and teaching of the Veda," says Nāka Maudgalya; for that indeed is austerity, that indeed is austerity.
Thus ends the ninth section.

Since it has been stated that "one attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) from consciousness alone," it might follow that the rituals prescribed by the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti* are rendered useless. To prevent this conclusion, these [rituals] are introduced here in order to demonstrate that they serve as means toward the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). "Truth" (*ṛta*) has already been explained. "Self-study" (*svādhyāya*) is the act of studying [the Veda]. "Proclamation" (*pravacana*) is teaching or the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). The ellipsis of the sentence is: "These, beginning with truth, are to be performed."

Truth is truthful speech, or austerity (*tapas*) such as the *kṛcchra* penance, according to the meaning already explained. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the pacification of the external organs; tranquility (*śama*) is the pacification of the internal organ. The sacred fires are to be consecrated; the *agnihotra* sacrifice is to be offered; and guests are to be honored. "Human" refers to worldly social conduct, and that should be performed as it has come down by tradition. If there are offspring, they are to be protected; and procreation (*prajana*) means approaching one’s wife during her fertile period.

"Procreation" means the birth of a grandson; [the phrase] "the son is to be settled" refers to this. Although one may be engaged in all these duties, the study and teaching of the Veda (*svādhyāya-pravacana*) must be performed with diligent effort; it is for this purpose that the study and teaching of the Veda are mentioned alongside everything else. For the knowledge of the meaning depends upon the study of the Veda, and the supreme good depends upon the knowledge of the meaning. Furthermore, teaching is for the sake of not forgetting that [knowledge] and for the sake of the increase of Dharma.

Therefore, one should apply oneself with diligence to the study and recitation of the Veda. "Satyavacas" means one whose speech is truth; that is, one who must practice only the truth—or this may be his name. "Rāthītara" refers to a teacher of the Rathītara lineage; he maintains that austerity alone must be practiced. "Taponitya" means one who is constant in austerity, devoted to austerity, or one for whom austerity is the highest goal—or this may be his name.

Pauruśiṣṭi, the son of Puruśiṣṭha, maintains that the teacher [is right]; that is, he holds that only the private study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) and its recitation (*pravacana*) are to be performed. Nāka by name, the son of Mudgala—Maudgalya—the teacher maintains [the same]. "For that is austerity, for that is austerity": because *svādhyāya* and *pravacana* alone are austerity, therefore they alone are to be performed. Although truth, austerity, *svādhyāya*, and *pravacana* have already been mentioned, their repetition here is for the sake of showing special regard.
Thus ends the ninth section.

"I am the shaker of the tree; my fame is like the ridge of a mountain. With my purifier raised high, like a prize-winning steed, I am my own nectar—wealthful and resplendent, wise and sprinkled with immortality. Thus is the Vedic recitation of Triśaṅku.
Thus ends the tenth section.

The traditional recitation of the mantra "I am the impeller of the tree" (*ahaṃ vṛkṣasya rerivā*) is for the purpose of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), and Vedic study is for the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), according to the context; for this entire section has knowledge as its purpose, and no other purpose is perceived. Furthermore, the arising of knowledge is logically possible for one whose being is purified by Vedic study. [The meaning is: "I am the impeller (*rerivā*)—the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) who sets it in motion—of the tree, that is, of the tree of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-vṛkṣa*) which is characterized by destruction. My fame (*kīrtiḥ*), that is, my renown (*khyātiḥ*), is as elevated as the summit of a mountain."

"Ūrdhvapavitra": that whose purifier (*pavitra*), the cause (*kāraṇa*) which is upward-pointing—that is, the supreme Brahman revealed by knowledge—is the purifier of me, the Self of all; such am I, "ūrdhvapavitra. "Vājinīva" means like Savitṛ who possesses *vāja* (food). Just as the immortal reality (*amṛta*), the pure essence of the Self, is well-known in Savitṛ through hundreds of Śruti and Smṛti texts, even so am I my own immortal, beautiful, and pure essence of the Self. I exist as such.

"Draviṇam" means wealth; "savarcasam" means radiant or luminous. That very thing follows [the thought]: "I am that reality of the Self. Alternatively, the knowledge of Brahman is "savarcasam" because it illuminates the reality of the Self. It is called "draviṇam" (wealth) because, like wealth, it is the cause of the bliss of liberation. In this interpretation, the phrase "has been obtained by me" must be supplied. "Sumedhāḥ": I am one whose intelligence ("medhā") is excellent ("su-"), characterized by omniscience. One possesses such "sumedhastva" through the application of skill in the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Therefore, he is "immortal" (*amṛta*), meaning one whose nature is not subject to death, who is undecaying (*akṣita*), inexhaustible (*avyaya*), or one who has been sprinkled (*ukṣita*) with the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*). This is according to the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "I have been sprinkled with the nectar of immortality. Thus, this is the "recitation of the Veda" (*vedānuvacana*) of the seer Triśaṅku, who has become Brahman and is a knower of Brahman. Here, "Veda" refers to the knowledge (*vedana*) consisting of the realization of the oneness of the Self; "recitation of the Veda" is the proclamation following the attainment of that [knowledge].

The meaning is that, like Vāmadeva, for the sake of proclaiming one's own state of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatā*), the traditional collection of mantras (*mantrāmnāya*)—the vision seen through the seer Triśaṅku—is a revelation of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). Furthermore, its recitation is understood to be for the purpose of the arising of that knowledge. This is understood from the fact that after the presentation of duties such as "Truth (*ṛta*) and so forth," there follows the recitation of the Veda (*vedānuvacana*).

Thus, for one who is engaged in the obligatory rites of the Śruti and Smṛti, who is free from desire, and who desires to know the Supreme Brahman, the visions of the seers (*ārṣāṇi darśanāni*) concerning the Self and other subjects manifest.
Thus ends the tenth section. 10.

Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs his pupil: "Speak the truth. Practice righteousness. Do not neglect your private Vedic study. Having brought wealth pleasing to your teacher, do not let the thread of progeny be cut off. One must not swerve from the truth. One must not swerve from righteousness. One must not swerve from what is beneficial. One must not swerve from prosperity. One must not swerve from private Vedic study and its recitation."

One must not neglect the rites for the gods and the ancestors. Be one who regards the mother as a god; be one who regards the father as a god; be one who regards the teacher as a god; be one who regards the guest as a god. Those actions which are blameless should be practiced, and not others. Those well-conducted practices of ours should be emulated by you.

Not others. Whatever Brahmins there may be who are more excellent and superior, you should offer them a seat. One should give with faith; one should not give without faith. One should give with dignity; one should give with modesty; one should give out of fear; one should give with a sense of obligation. Now, if you should have any doubt regarding your ritual action or any doubt regarding your conduct—

In that regard, those Brahmins who are discerning, diligent, attentive, free from harshness, and lovers of dharma—just as they would conduct themselves there, so should you conduct yourself there. Furthermore, regarding those who have been falsely accused: those Brahmins who are discerning, diligent, attentive, free from harshness, and lovers of dharma—just as they would conduct themselves toward them, so should you conduct yourself toward them. This is the instruction; this is the teaching; this is the secret doctrine of the Veda (*vedopaniṣad*); this is the precept. Thus it should be honored; thus indeed should it be honored.
Thus ends the eleventh section. 11.

The commencement of the instruction on duties, beginning with the words "Having studied the Veda," has the following purpose: that Śrauta and Smārta rites must necessarily be performed prior to the realization of Brahman. This is because the scriptural injunction to "instruct" (anuśāsana) is for the sake of purifying the person; for in one whose being is purified through such refinement, knowledge of the Self arises easily. As the Smṛti states: "By austerity one destroys impurity; by knowledge one attains immortality" (Manu 12.104).

And it will be said: "Seek to know Brahman through austerity" (TaittU 3.2–3.5). Therefore, ritual actions are to be performed for the sake of the arising of knowledge. From the word *anuśāsana* ("instruction"), as in the phrase "he instructs," it follows that a fault arises from transgressing the instruction. Furthermore, because they are introduced earlier—prior to the commencement of the exclusive knowledge of Brahman—the ritual actions are presented first.

And when the knowledge of Brahman has arisen, one finds fearless stability (TaittU 2.7.1); "one does not fear from anything" (TaittU 2.9.1); and by such passages as "Why have I not performed what is good? (TaittU 2.9.1), [the text] will demonstrate the cessation of ritual action (*karmanaiṣkiñcanya*). Therefore, it is understood that rituals serve to produce knowledge by means of destroying previously accumulated evil. And from the wording of a mantra: "Having crossed over death by means of ignorance, one attains immortality by means of knowledge" (ĪU 11).

The instruction regarding the *ṛta* and other duties in the preceding section was for the purpose of avoiding futility; here, however, since it serves the purpose of generating knowledge, it is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) on what must be performed. "Having recited"—that is, having taught—the Veda, the teacher instructs the student (*antevāsin*), meaning he teaches him subsequent to the grasping of the text, causing him to comprehend its meaning. From this it is understood that one who has studied the Veda should not return from the teacher’s house without having undertaken the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*). This is also supported by the Smṛti: "Having understood [the Veda], one should undertake ritual acts."

How does he instruct? He says: "Speak the truth"—that which is to be spoken must be stated exactly as it is known through valid means of cognition; speak that. "Practice dharma"—the term 'dharma' is a general designation for those things to be performed, since specific instances such as truthfulness have already been mentioned. "Do not neglect your private recitation"—do not be negligent regarding the study [of the Veda].

Having brought and given to the teacher wealth that is dear and desired for the sake of the teacher, as payment for his knowledge, and having been permitted by the teacher, one should take a suitable wife and not cut off the thread of progeny—the continuity of offspring must not be interrupted. The intention is that even if a son has not yet been born, one should make an effort to produce one through such rites as the *putrakāmya* (desire for a son), because of the force of the mention of the three terms: *prajā* (progeny), *prajanana* (procreation), and *prajāti* (lineage).

Otherwise, he would have stated only this one [injunction]: "and procreation. Regarding the phrase "one must not be negligent toward truth" (*satyān na pramaditavyam*), negligence means that one must not commit an error; and negligence toward truth consists in falling into falsehood, by virtue of the force of the word "negligence" (*pramāda*). The meaning is that one must not speak untruth even through forgetfulness; otherwise, there would merely be a prohibition against speaking untruth. [Likewise,] "one must not be negligent toward dharma" (*dharmān na pramaditavyam*).

Since the word *dharma* refers to that which is to be performed, negligence regarding it is an error; one must not be negligent, meaning that *dharma* is indeed to be practiced. Thus, one must not be negligent regarding wholesome actions that serve to protect oneself. Regarding prosperity—that is, abundant success—one must not be negligent regarding auspicious actions intended for that prosperity. One must not be negligent regarding the study and recitation of the Vedas.

*Śvādhyāya* is study and *pravacana* is teaching; one must not neglect these two. The meaning is that these indeed must be performed as obligatory duties. Likewise, one must not neglect the rites for the gods and the ancestors (*devapitṛkārya*); the rituals for the gods and the ancestors must be performed. "One whose god is his mother" (*mātṛdeva*) means you should become such a person—that is, one for whom the mother is a deity. In the same way, become one for whom the father is a deity, the teacher is a deity, and the guest is a deity. The meaning is that these are to be honored like deities.

Furthermore, whatever other blameless and irreproachable actions are characterized by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), those should be cultivated and performed by you; others, which are faulty even if performed by the learned, should not be done. Those very practices of our teachers that are well-conducted, beautiful deeds, and not in contradiction with the Vedas (*āmnāya*) and so forth—those alone should be attended to by you and carried out for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); that is to say, they must be performed as a rule. Not others, even if performed by the teachers, that are of the opposite nature.

Whosoever are distinguished by qualities such as being a teacher (*ācārya*) and are superior (*śreyāṃsaḥ*) or more praiseworthy (*praśasyatarāḥ*) than we or those like us—those are Brāhmaṇas, not Kṣatriyas and the rest. Toward them, you should "breathe out" (*praśvasitavyam*) by means of their seat, that is, by giving them a seat and so forth. "Breathing out" (*praśvāsaḥ*) means the removal of fatigue; the meaning is that their fatigue must be removed by you. When they have gathered for a session (*āsane*) for the purpose of a social assembly (*goṣṭhī*), you should not "breathe out" toward them—not even a mere breath of relief should be directed at them.

One should simply grasp the essence of what has been said. Furthermore, whatever is to be given must be given with faith; that which is not to be given out of lack of faith should not be given. One should give with prosperity and abundance, and one should give with modesty and shame, and one should give with fear and dread, as well as with mindfulness. Mindfulness refers to tasks such as those concerning mantras and the like.

Now, if while you are conducting yourself in this manner, at any time a doubt or uncertainty should arise regarding a rite prescribed by Śruti or Smṛti, or regarding conduct characterized by proper behavior—then those Brāhmaṇas who are "engaged" (yuktāḥ) in that place or at that time in such rites and so forth; this connection with the distant word must be made. They are "reflective" (sammarśinaḥ), meaning capable of deliberation. They are "engaged" (yuktāḥ), meaning devoted to ritual action or proper conduct. They are "unengaged" (ayuktāḥ), meaning not employed by others. They are "not harsh" (alūkṣāḥ), meaning not rough, possessing minds free from cruelty.

"Those who desire dharma, who seek the unseen goal, and who are not overcome by passion"—they should be such; those brahmins, in whatever manner and by whatever means they might conduct themselves in that action or in their livelihood, in that same way you also should conduct yourself. Furthermore, regarding those who have been falsely accused—those who have been charged with a fault by someone through a doubtful accusation—in their case as well, one should apply all that was said previously, beginning with "those who there... and so forth. This is the instruction, the rule.

This is the instruction for fathers and others toward their sons and others. This is the secret of the Veda (*vedopaniṣad*), the mystery of the Veda, and the meaning of the Veda; this alone is the teaching (*anuśāsana*), the word of the Lord, because the injunctive statement of the command has been declared. Or rather, this is the instruction of all that constitutes valid authority. Since this is so, therefore everything as stated should be meditated upon and performed.
The repetition—"this indeed is to be meditated upon, this indeed is to be meditated upon, and not not to be meditated upon"—is for the sake of showing reverence. (TaittUBh 1.11.4)

In this regard, it is considered for the sake of distinguishing between knowledge and action: whether the supreme good arises from actions alone, or from actions in conjunction with knowledge, or from both knowledge and action combined, or from knowledge dependent upon action, or indeed from knowledge alone. Among these, it might be argued that it arises from actions alone, because one who possesses knowledge of the entire meaning of the Veda is entitled to perform ritual action.

For there is a traditional teaching (smṛti): "The entire Veda, along with its secret portions (Upaniṣads), must be mastered by the twice-born" (Manu 2.165). And this mastery includes the meaning of the Upaniṣads, such as the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna) and so forth. Furthermore, in all instances, it is shown that only the learned person has the qualification for ritual action, as in the statements, "The learned one sacrifices" and "The learned one officiates at a sacrifice," and also in the principle that "performance follows from knowing. Moreover, some believe that the entire Veda is for the purpose of ritual action; if the supreme good were not attained through rituals, the Veda would be purposeless.

No, because liberation is eternal. For liberation is held to be eternal; and it is well known in the world that the product of action is non-eternal. If the highest good were to result from actions, it would be non-eternal, and that is undesirable. If it is argued that liberation does not depend on knowledge at all—since one does not undertake optional or prohibited actions, since actions already commenced are exhausted solely through experience, and since no transgression occurs due to the non-performance of obligatory duties—then that is not so.

It has already been refuted that the production of another body caused by that [ignorance] would follow from the possibility of residual karma (*śeṣakarman*), and that the destruction of such residual karma is impossible because it is not contradicted by the performance of obligatory duties (*nityānuṣṭhāna*). Furthermore, as for what was said—that one who possesses knowledge of the entire meaning of the Veda is qualified for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) and so forth—that is also not the case; for meditation (*upāsana*) is distinct from the knowledge derived from hearing the scriptures (*śrutajñāna*). Indeed, one is qualified for ritual action by means of mere scriptural knowledge alone; it does not depend upon meditation.

Furthermore, meditation (*upāsana*) is enjoined as something distinct from the knowledge derived from hearing (*śruta-jñāna*), having liberation as its fruit; and this distinction is established because it is well-known as a separate entity. Having stated that "it is to be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*), there is the injunction of other efforts distinct from that, namely, "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*) and "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*); thus, reflection and meditation are well-established as being distinct from the knowledge gained through hearing. If that is so, then liberation would result from ritual actions that depend upon such knowledge.

If it is argued that actions accompanied by knowledge possess the capacity to initiate a different effect—just as poisons, curd, and the like, though naturally capable of initiating effects such as death or fever, acquire the capacity to initiate a different effect when combined with mantras, sugar, and so forth; and thus liberation is initiated by actions accompanied by knowledge—this is not so. For the defect has already been stated: that which is produced (ārabhya) is non-eternal. If it is argued that even though it is produced, it is nonetheless eternal because of a scriptural statement, we say no; for a scriptural statement functions only as an indicator (jñāpaka).

Speech is that which makes known an object as it truly is; it does not create something non-existent. Indeed, even by means of a hundred words, the eternal cannot be commenced, nor can that which has been commenced become indestructible. By this, the claim that liberation is commenced by the combination of knowledge and action is refuted. If it is argued that knowledge and action merely remove the causes that obstruct liberation, we say no; for action is observed to have other fruits. Indeed, the fruits of action are seen to be origination, refinement, modification, and attainment.

Furthermore, liberation is the opposite of results such as birth and so forth. If it is argued that liberation is something to be attained because of scriptural texts concerning "going"—such as "through the gate of the sun" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.11) and "going upwards by those two" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3.16)—we say no. Because Brahman is all-pervading and because [the individual selves] are non-different from the goers; since Brahman is the cause of ether and the rest, it is all-pervading, and all conscious selves are non-distinct from Brahman. Therefore, liberation is not something to be attained.

The destination to be gone to must be a place distinct from the goer; for that which is non-different from something cannot be reached by that very same thing. And this non-difference is established from hundreds of scriptural and traditional texts, such as: "Having created that, he entered into it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), and "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.3). If it is argued that there is a contradiction with scriptural statements regarding movement and sovereignty, one might further object: "If liberation were unattainable, then [there would be no point in seeking it]."

If it be argued that there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "He becomes one-fold according to his movements and his learning" (ChU 7.26.2), "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers" (ChU 8.2.1), and "With women, or with vehicles" (ChU 8.12.3), and so forth—[we reply: No, for those [passages] have as their object the *kāryabrahman* (the effected Brahman). For women and the like may exist in the *kāryabrahman*, but not in the *kāraṇabrahman* (the causal Brahman), which is "one only, without a second" (ChU 6.2.1), and wherein "he sees nothing else" (ChU 7.24.1); for how could he see anything, and by what means? (BAU 2.4.14).

This is because of such scriptural passages as [Chāndogya Upaniṣad] 4.5.15. Furthermore, due to their mutual contradiction, the combination of knowledge and ritual action is untenable. For knowledge—which has as its object the true reality in which specific factors of action such as the agent have been dissolved—is in contradiction with ritual action, which is accomplished by means of those very factors that are the opposite of such knowledge. Indeed, it is impossible for a single entity to be perceived in two ways—as possessing specific distinctions such as agency from the perspective of ultimate reality, and simultaneously as being devoid of them.

For one of the two must necessarily be false, and since the falsity of one follows, it is logical that duality—which is the object of innate ignorance—is false. For it is said: "Where there is, as it were, duality" (BĀU 2.4.14; 4.5.15); "He goes from death to death who perceives therein any diversity" (KaU 2.1.10/4.10); and "But where one sees another... (BĀU 4.3.23).

This is known from hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "That is small" (ChU 7.24.1); "He thinks, 'He is one and I am another'" (BĀU 1.4.10); and "He makes a distinction within himself; then fear comes upon him" (TaittU 2.7). And the reality of oneness is established by such scriptural passages as: "It should be viewed as one alone" (BĀU 4.4.20); "One only, without a second" (ChU 6.2.1); "All this is indeed Brahman" (MU 2.2.11); and "All this is indeed the Self" (ChU 7.25.2).

Furthermore, when the distinctions between the various factors of action (kārakas), such as the recipient (sampradāna) and so forth, are not perceived, the status of an "object" (karman) is not possible. Moreover, thousands of scriptural passages are heard regarding the domain of knowledge (vidyā) that negate the perception of otherness. Therefore, there is a contradiction between knowledge and ritual action; consequently, their combination (samuccaya) is untenable.

In this regard, as for what was said—that liberation results from knowledge and action combined—that is untenable, because actions are enjoined. If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the Śruti: if the realization of the oneness of the Self is enjoined by subverting specific causal factors such as the agent and so forth—just like the cognition of a rope-substrate which subverts the erroneous cognition of a snake and the like—then a contradiction arises because the injunctions regarding ritual action would be rendered devoid of an object. Yet, ritual actions have been enjoined; and that contradiction is not tenable.

If it is argued that this is because the Vedas are authoritative, we say no; for the Vedas have as their primary purpose the instruction regarding the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). To begin with, the Veda is intent on instructing in knowledge (*vidyā*) in the sense that "the person must be liberated from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)," and thus it proceeds by revealing knowledge so that the cessation of ignorance—the cause of transmigratory existence—may be accomplished. Therefore, there is no contradiction. If it is further argued that even so, the scripture which teaches the existence of causal factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth remains contradictory, we say no.

The scripture, relying on the very existence of the factors of action (*kāraka*) as they are attained, prescribes ritual actions for the sake of exhausting accumulated demerit for those seeking liberation, and serves as the means for attaining results for those desiring fruits. For the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is not possible for one whose progress is obstructed by accumulated demerit; when that is exhausted, knowledge arises, from which follows the cessation of ignorance, and from that, the absolute end of saṃsāra. Furthermore, for one who perceives no self (*anātman*), desire has the non-self as its object.

One who possesses desire performs actions; from that arises *saṃsāra*, characterized by the appropriation of a body and so forth for the sake of experiencing their fruits. For one who perceives the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*), however, there is no production of desire because, in the absence of objects distinct from that [Self], there is no basis for desire; and since nothing exists apart from the Self, when desire does not arise, abiding in one's own Self is liberation (*mokṣa*). Therefore, knowledge and action are in opposition. Precisely because of this opposition, knowledge does not depend upon actions with respect to liberation.

However, with respect to the attainment of one's own Self, obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) serve as a cause for knowledge by means of removing the obstructions of previously accumulated sins; it is for this reason that we stated that the rites were introduced in this context. Thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptural injunctions regarding ritual action. Therefore, it is established that supreme bliss results from knowledge alone.

If that were so, then the existence of other stages of life (*āśrama*) would be untenable, because the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is caused by ritual action (*karman*), and such actions are prescribed for the householder stage alone; thus, there would be only a single stage of life. Consequently, scriptural injunctions such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvaj jīva*) would be more consistent [with this view]. [Reply: No, because ritual actions are manifold. For ritual actions do not consist solely of the *agnihotra* and the like.

Furthermore, there exist such actions as celibacy, austerity, speaking the truth, tranquility, self-control, non-violence, and so forth—which are well-known in the later stages of life (*uttarāśrama*)—that are unmixed and most effective for the arising of knowledge, as well as those characterized by meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and the like. And the author will state: "Seek to know Brahman through austerity" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.2.1; 3.5.1).

Furthermore, since the arising of knowledge is possible even prior to entering the householder stage due to actions performed in previous lives, and since the adoption of the householder stage is for the sake of performing ritual action, the adoption of the householder stage would be utterly purposeless if knowledge were to be accomplished through ritual action; moreover, sons and the like exist for the sake of the world.

Furthermore, for one whose desires have turned away from these ends to be accomplished through sons and so forth—namely, this world, the world of the ancestors, and the world of the gods—and who perceives the eternally established Self and thus sees no purpose in ritual action, how can engagement in such action be justified? Even for one who has entered the householder stage, once knowledge has arisen and he becomes dispassionate toward actions through the maturation of that knowledge, seeing no purpose in rituals, there would necessarily be a cessation from all actions.

If it is argued that [renunciation] is improper because of the observation of scriptural indications such as, "O Maitreyī, I am about to depart from this state" (BĀU 4.5.2), and because one observes an excessive effort on the part of the Śruti regarding ritual action—namely, that there is greater effort toward rituals like the Agnihotra, and that great exertion is required for such rites since they must be accomplished through numerous means—[we reply: no.

If it is argued that because austerity (*tapas*)—consisting of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and other such duties—is common to the householder stage as well as the other stages of life, and because the other stages require fewer means, it is not appropriate for those in the other stages to have an equal option regarding it as the householder does, we say no. This is because of the assistance rendered by actions performed in previous lives. As for what was said—that there is greater effort required for ritual action (*karman*) according to scripture and so forth—that is not a fault.

For even actions performed in previous births—characterized by the Agnihotra sacrifice and the like, as well as those characterized by celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth—become supportive toward the arising of knowledge. This is because some are seen to be detached from birth itself, while others are engaged in ritual acts, lacking detachment and being hostile to knowledge. Therefore, for those who are detached due to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) formed in previous births, the attainment of another stage of life (*āśrama*) is indeed desired, both because of their detachment and because of the abundance of the fruits of ritual action.

Because the fruits of action—characterized by sons, heaven, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and so forth—are innumerable, and because men have many desires regarding them, it is appropriate that the Śruti exerts greater effort toward those actions. This is seen from the abundance of prayers such as, "May this be mine, may that be mine. Furthermore, it is because they are the means; for we have already stated that actions are the means to knowledge (*vidyā*). Greater effort must be applied to the means, not to the end.

If it is argued that because knowledge (*vidyā*) has action as its cause, other efforts are useless—namely, that if knowledge arises solely from actions through the destruction of the obstructions consisting of previously accumulated sins, then the effort of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, which is taught separately from actions in the *Upaniṣads*, is purposeless—the answer is no, because there is no such restrictive rule. For there is no fixed rule that knowledge arises only from the destruction of obstructions, and not rather from the grace of the Lord (*īśvara*), the performance of austerity (*tapas*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth.

Furthermore, because non-violence, celibacy, and so forth are supportive of knowledge (*vidyā*), and because hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are its direct causes, the other stages of life (*āśrama*) are established. It is thus proven that all [stages] have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for knowledge, and that the supreme good consists solely in knowledge itself.

May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious to us; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Salutations to Brahman! Salutations to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. To you alone, the perceptible Brahman, have I spoken. I have spoken the *ṛta*; I have spoken the truth.
