May that protect me; may that protect the speaker. It has protected me; it has protected the speaker. *Oṃ*. Peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the twelfth section. 12.

For the purpose of pacifying the obstacles encountered in attaining past knowledge, he recites the *śānti* prayer beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us. This has been explained previously. Thus ends the Chapter on Training (*śikṣādhyāya*).

May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious to us. May Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us. May Viṣṇu, the wide-striding, be auspicious to us. Homage to Brahman! Homage to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the manifest Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as the manifest Brahman. I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Truth. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker. Om! Peace! Peace! Peace!
Thus ends the twelfth section. 12.

The Brahmānanda Vallī Oṃ. May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious to us. May Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us. May Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Salutations to Brahman! Salutations to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Satya. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker. Oṃ! May it protect us both together; may it nourish us both together.

"Let us two perform [this] with vigor; may our study be brilliant; may we not hate each other. Om! Peace! Peace! Peace! The *śānti* (propitiatory prayer) beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us" was recited previously for the purpose of pacifying obstacles to the attainment of the knowledge already passed. Now, however, the *śānti* beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us" and "May He protect us both" is recited for the purpose of pacifying obstacles to the attainment of the Brahma-knowledge that is about to be taught. The passage beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us" is clear, as before.

May He protect us both—the disciple and the teacher—together; may He protect us together. May He nourish us both with the Brahman. May we together perform our work—that is, may we accomplish our capacity for knowledge and so forth. May what is studied by us two, who are radiant, be radiant; that is to say, may it be fit for the understanding of its meaning.

"May we not hate each other. Since hatred might arise between the disciple and the teacher due to negligence regarding some injustice committed for the sake of acquiring knowledge, this benediction—"may we not hate each other"—is intended to pacify that. "May we never fall into mutual enmity. The threefold repetition of "Peace! Peace! Peace! has already been explained. Furthermore, this peace is for the purpose of pacifying obstacles to the knowledge about to be taught. The attainment of the science of the Self is desired without obstacle, for that is the root of the supreme good.

*Oṃ*. "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Regarding this, there is this verse: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. He who knows it as hidden in the secret cave of the heart, in the highest heaven—he, together with the wise Brahman, attains all desires. From that very Self, indeed, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; and from food, the person (*puruṣa*).

Now, this person consists of the essence of food. Of him, this is the head; this is the right wing; this is the left wing; this is the trunk; and this is the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the first section (anuvāka). 1.

Meditations concerning the *saṃhitā* and other such topics, which are not in conflict with ritual actions, have been taught. Immediately following that, the vision of the Self as possessing internal limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) was taught by means of the *vyāhṛtis*, with self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) as its fruit. However, since the seed of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is not entirely destroyed by this much alone, this [section] beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" is commenced for the purpose of removing ignorance—the seed of all calamities—and for the sake of the vision of the Self in which all specific limiting adjuncts have been shaken off.

The purpose of this knowledge of Brahman is the cessation of ignorance, and from that follows the absolute absence of saṃsāra. And the text will say: "The knower does not fear anything from any quarter" (TaittU 2.9.1). For if the cause of saṃsāra were present, it would be untenable [to say] "he finds fearlessness and a firm foundation" (TaittU 2.7.1), as well as [the statement] "evil and merit, done and undone, do not afflict him."

From this it is understood that from this consciousness—which has as its object Brahman, the Self of all—there follows the absolute non-existence of *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, [the author] himself stated the purpose at the very beginning with the words "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," for the sake of making known the relationship and the purpose. For once the relationship and the purpose are fully understood, one proceeds toward the hearing, grasping, retaining, and repeated practice of the knowledge (*vidyā*). Indeed, the fruit of knowledge is preceded by hearing and so forth, according to the text: "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (BĀU 2.4.5).

This is established by other scriptural passages such as these. "The knower of Brahman" refers to one who knows—that is, fully realizes—Brahman, whose characteristics will be described later; it is called *brahman* because of its supreme vastness (*bṛhattama*). Such a knower of Brahman attains the Supreme, which is unsurpassed; that very Brahman is the Supreme. For there can be no attainment of one thing through the knowledge of another.

Furthermore, another scripture clearly shows that the attainment of Brahman belongs only to the knower of Brahman: "He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and so forth (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).

But will not the scripture declare that Brahman is all-pervading and the very self of all? Therefore, it cannot be attained; for attainment is observed to occur only between one delimited thing and another delimited thing. Since Brahman is undivided and the self of all, its attainment—being like that of something delimited and non-self—is logically impossible. This is not a fault. Why? Because the attainment or non-attainment of Brahman depends upon perception and non-perception.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), although this individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of Brahman, it perceives itself as having a self consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth—externally delimited by the elements (*bhūtamātra*)—and its mind remains attached thereto.

Just as one who completes a given number [of items] fails to perceive his own nature because his mind is attached to external objects to be counted—even though he is not separated from himself—so too, through ignorance (*avidyā*), which is characterized by the non-perception of the nature of the supreme Brahman, one has accepted the external, non-self entities such as those consisting of food (*annamaya*) as the self; consequently, one conceives, "I am not other than these non-self entities such as those consisting of food. In this way, although Brahman is one's very own self, it remains unattained due to ignorance.

Just as for that very Self—which, through ignorance, had not attained its true nature as Brahman, which was the one completing the aforementioned number, and which, though unattained due to ignorance, was later remembered by someone—there is once again the attainment of that same [Self] through knowledge (*vidyā*); so too, the attainment of Brahman, the Universal Self taught in the Śruti, is indeed logically established through the knowledge arising from the vision of it as one's own Self. The statement, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), serves as the aphorism for the entire meaning of this section.

By means of this sentence, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (TaittU 2.1.1), there is first a general determination of the nature of Brahman—which was introduced as the object to be known—by stating its definition capable of imparting a specific nature that distinguishes it from everything else; and for the sake of specifically knowing that very Brahman, whose nature has been thus defined and whose fruit is the knowledge of Brahman, as being non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) through the mode of its own essential identity.

The characteristic of attaining the Supreme Brahman has been stated; however, this verse is cited to demonstrate that this state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmabhāva*) is nothing other than the very nature of Brahman, which transcends all the attributes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Regarding this, it is said: "On this point, this verse is recited" (*tad eṣābhyuktā*). That is to say, on the very subject matter expressed in the Brāhmaṇa passage, this verse is recited and handed down. The statement, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma*), is the definition of Brahman.

For the three words beginning with "truth" (*satya*) are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the qualified (*viśeṣya*), which is Brahman. Brahman is the qualified because it is intended as the object to be known; since Brahman is intended primarily as that which is to be known, it must be understood as the qualified. Therefore, precisely because of this relationship between qualifier and qualified, the words beginning with "truth," ending in the same case-ending, are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

Brahman, when qualified by the three qualifiers beginning with "truth," is distinguished from other objects of qualification; for it is thus known when it has been distinguished from others, just as in the world one says, "a blue, large, beautiful lotus."

[Objection: Is it not the case that a qualificand is qualified by another qualifier when it deviates from it, as in "the blue and the red lotus"? For when there are multiple substances of the same genus possessing multiple qualifiers, then the qualifier has meaning. This is because a qualifier cannot apply to another [substance] within a single entity, as in the case of "this one sun"; likewise, Brahman is only one, and there are no other Brahmans by which it might be qualified, as in the case of a blue lotus. [Reply: No.

Because qualifiers have the purpose of defining, this fault does not apply. Why? Because qualifiers are primarily intended for the purpose of definition (*lakṣaṇa*), not because they are primarily intended as qualifiers themselves. What, then, is the distinction between a definition and that which is defined, or between a qualifier and that which is qualified? It is said: qualifiers exclude the qualified only from things of the same class, whereas a definition excludes it from everything; for example, "space is that which provides room. And we have already stated that a sentence has the purpose of providing a definition.

The words "truth" and so forth are not mutually connected, because they are for the sake of another; for they have as their referent the qualified object [Brahman]. Therefore, each qualifying word, independent of the others, is connected with the word "Brahman": "Brahman is truth," "Brahman is knowledge," "Brahman is infinite. That which, having been determined by a certain form, does not deviate from that form, is "existent" (sat) and "truth" (satya). That which, having been determined by a certain form, deviates from that form, is called "unreal" (anṛta).

Therefore, "the modification is unreal, a mere handle of speech; the modification is a mere name; 'clay' alone is the truth" (ChU 6.1.4). Because of this restriction that only Being (*sat*) is real, Brahman is established as the Truth. Consequently, Brahman is determined to be the cause. And since a cause possesses the nature of an agent, and because it is a real entity, it would follow—like clay—that it is insentient in nature. Therefore, it is said: "Brahman is knowledge."

Knowledge (*jñāna*) means cognition (*jñapti*), awakening (*avabodha*); the word *jñāna* is derived as a state (*bhāva-sādhana*), not as the agent of knowledge, because it functions as an attribute of Brahman along with "truth" (*satya*) and "infinitude" (*ananta*). Indeed, truth and infinitude are not possible if [Brahman] were the agent of knowledge. For if it were undergoing modification through being the agent of knowledge, how could it be true and infinite? That which is not divided from anything is infinite; and if it were the agent of knowledge, it would be divided from the object of knowledge and the act of knowing, and thus its infinitude would not exist.

This is because of another scriptural passage: "Where one knows nothing else, that is the Infinite (bhūman); but where one knows something else, that is the finite" (ChU 7.24.1). If it is argued that the phrase "one knows nothing else" implies a prohibition of specific objects while implying that one knows the Self, we say no; for the sentence is intended to enjoin the definition of the Infinite. The passage beginning with "where one sees nothing else" (ChU 7.24.1) is a statement intended to enjoin the defining characteristics of the Infinite.

Based on the well-known fact that one perceives another, the nature of the Infinite (*bhūman*) is made known there where that [perception] does not exist; for the mention of "another" serves to negate what has been previously established, and thus the statement is not intended to imply the existence of an action within itself. Furthermore, since there is no differentiation within itself, cognition is impossible regarding the self. Moreover, if the Self were an object of knowledge, it would follow that there is no knower, because it would already be fully occupied as the object of knowledge.

If it is argued that the Self is one and the same, yet exists in two ways—as both the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the knower (*jñātṛ*), we say no; because it is partless, it cannot simultaneously be both the object and the subject of knowledge. Indeed, for that which is without parts, the simultaneous status of being both the known and the knower is impossible. Furthermore, if the Self were an object of cognition like a jar or other such things, the instruction on knowledge would be purposeless; for an instruction on knowledge is not meaningful for that which is already well-known like a jar. Therefore, if the Self were a knower, its infinity could not be established. Moreover, its being pure existence (*sanmātratva*) is untenable as long as it possesses specific attributes such as being the agent of knowledge.

And being "pure existence" (*sanmātratva*) is its reality, according to another scriptural passage: "That is the Truth" (*ChU* 6.7.7). Therefore, because the word *jñāna* is employed as a qualifier together with the words "Truth" (*satya*) and "Infinite" (*ananta*), the word *jñāna* here functions as a noun denoting a state of being (*bhāvasādhana*). The expression "Brahman is knowledge" (*jñānaṃ brahma*) is used to exclude [the Brahman] from being an agent or other grammatical factors (*kāraka*), and to exclude its having an insentient nature (*acidrūpatā*), like clay and such things. From the statement "Brahman is knowledge," the quality of finitude might be inferred, since ordinary knowledge is observed to be finite.

Therefore, in order to exclude that [misconception], he says "infinite" (*anantam*). Since terms such as "real" (*satya*) have the purpose of excluding attributes such as "unreal," and since the qualificand, Brahman, is not commonly known—just like a blue lotus and so forth—it might be argued that the statement beginning with "real" results in a meaning of mere emptiness, like this: "Here comes the son of a barren woman, having bathed in the waters of a mirage, wearing a crest made of sky-flowers, and bearing a bow made of a hare's horn. This is not so, because [the terms] serve the purpose of providing a definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

We have already stated that even though terms such as "truth" (*satya*) function as qualifiers, their primary purpose is to serve as a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). For if the object to be defined were empty, the statement of its definition would be meaningless; therefore, because they serve the purpose of definition, we consider them not to have emptiness as their referent. Furthermore, even when "truth" and the other terms function as qualifiers, they do not abandon their own inherent meanings. Indeed, if the words "truth" and so forth had emptiness as their referent, they could not logically act as restrictors of the object to be qualified.

But if [the terms] possess meaning through their referents such as "truth" (satya) and so forth, then the status of Brahman—the subject—as the controller is established in contrast to other subjects possessing qualities opposite to those. Furthermore, the word *brahman* is indeed meaningful by virtue of its own primary sense. In that context, the word *ananta* (infinite) functions as a qualifier by means of the negation of finitude (*antavattva*), whereas the words *satya* (truth) and *jñāna* (knowledge) function as qualifiers by directly imparting their own respective meanings.

Therefore, from the phrase "from this very Self," because the word "Self" is applied specifically to Brahman, Brahman is indeed the Self of the knower. Furthermore, the texts demonstrate its nature as the Self in such passages as, "He reaches this Self consisting of bliss," and by showing its entry into that [body], as in, "Having created that, He entered into it" (TaittU 2.6.1), which shows that very same Being entering the body in the form of the individual soul (jīva). Thus, the true nature of the knower is Brahman.

If that is the case, then because it possesses the nature of a self (*ātmatva*), it must be the agent of knowledge; for it is well known that "the self is the knower. Furthermore, the statement "it is without desire" establishes the agency of knowledge for one who possesses desire. Therefore, it is untenable to say that Brahman is pure consciousness (*jñapti*) on the grounds of being the agent of knowledge, as this would entail the consequence of impermanence. Even if Brahman were of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpatā*) such that consciousness is its knowledge, impermanence would still follow, as would dependence upon other factors; for verbal roots require their respective factors of action (*kāraka*), and knowledge is the meaning of a verbal root.

Therefore, it [the self] would possess impermanence and dependence; this is not so, because the designation "being an effect" is applied to it without being distinct from its own nature. The nature of the self is consciousness (*jñapti*), and since it is not separate from that, it is indeed eternal. Nevertheless, those appearances in the form of sound and other objects—which belong to the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and which transform into the forms of objects through the doors of the eyes and other senses—become the objects of the self’s cognition. Even as they arise, they arise already pervaded by the self’s cognition.

Therefore, those things which are illuminated by the cognition of the Self, which are denoted by the word "cognition," and which constitute the meaning of the verbal roots [of action], are imagined by the undiscriminating to be the very attributes of the Self in the form of modifications. However, that which is the cognition of Brahman—like the light of the sun or the heat of fire—is non-different from the nature of Brahman; it is the very essence itself. It does not depend upon any other cause.

Because all entities have that as their eternal nature, because they are not distinct from it in terms of space and time, because it is the cause of time, space, and so forth, and because it is supremely subtle, there exists nothing else—whether subtle, hidden, remote, past, present, or future—that is unknowable to it. Therefore, that Brahman is omniscient. And the words of the Mantras declare: "Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes, he hears without ears."

"He knows the knowable, yet there is no knower of him; they call him the foremost, the great Person" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19); and from such scriptural passages as, "For there is no loss of the consciousness of the conscious one, because of its imperishability; nor is there a second thing existing apart from it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30). Since the nature of the knower is not distinct [from Brahman], and since Brahman does not depend on instruments or other causal conditions, its status as the very nature of knowledge is established as eternal. Therefore, it is certainly not the meaning of a verbal root, because it is not of the nature of an action.

For this very reason, Brahman is not the agent of knowledge; and for that same reason, it is not even denotable by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Nevertheless, it is indicated—though not directly expressed—by the word "knowledge," which refers to a property of the intellect (*buddhi*) and appears as its reflection, because Brahman is devoid of properties such as genus (*jāti*), which serve as the grounds for the application of words. The same applies to the word "truth" (*satya*). Since the essential nature of Brahman is the total cessation of all particularities, it is indicated by the word "truth"—which has as its object the universal of external existence—as "Brahman is truth."

But Brahman is not merely that which is denoted by the word "truth" (*satya*). Thus, words such as "truth" and so forth, through their mutual proximity, become mutually restrictive and restricted; being thus, they serve to exclude [the literal meanings] from that which is denoted by words like "truth," and they function as indicators (*lakṣaṇārtha*) of Brahman. Therefore, it is established that Brahman is inexpressible, as stated in the passages: "from which speech turns back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it" (TaittU 2.4.1; 2.9.1), and "unexpounded, without abode" (TaittU 2.7.1); furthermore, Brahman is not the meaning of a sentence (*avākyārtha*), just as a blue lotus is.

He who knows—that is, understands—that Brahman thus explained, which is situated and established in the *guhā*. [The word] *guhā* [is derived from] the root *guh*, meaning "to conceal. It is called *guhā* because the objects of knowledge—the knowable and the knower—are hidden within it; or alternatively, because the two goals of human existence, enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), are hidden within it. That *guhā* is the intellect (*buddhi*). Within that, in the supreme, most excellent *vyoman*—the space known as the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*)—it resides. For that is the supreme space, as stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (3.8.11): "In this very Imperishable (*akṣara*), O Gārgī, is the space," due to its proximity to the Imperishable.

Alternatively, because of the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the phrase "in the cave, in the sky," the unmanifested space (avyākṛtākāśa) itself is the cave; for even there, all things are hidden throughout the three periods of time, owing to its being the cause and its extreme subtlety. Within that is Brahman deposited. However, it is more logical that the supreme sky is indeed the space within the heart (hārdam), since the sky is intended here as a constituent part of knowledge (vijñāna).

The supreme nature of the space within the heart is well-established from another scriptural passage: "That which is the space outside a person, that which is the space inside a person, and that which is the space within the heart" (ChU 3.12.7). In that space within the heart, there is the intellect, which is the cave; in that [intellect], Brahman is deposited, and it is perceived as distinct through the exclusion of that [intellect]. For otherwise, there could be no connection with a specific place or time for Brahman, because it is all-pervading and devoid of distinctions.

Knowing Brahman in this way, what does he say? He "attains" or "enjoys" all desires—that is, all objects of enjoyment—without exception. Is it like those of us [ordinary people], who experience sons, heaven, and so forth in succession? No; he says they are "together," meaning simultaneously, mounted upon a single moment by means of a single perception, which is eternal like the light of the sun and non-different from the very nature of Brahman, that which we described as "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (TaittU 2.1.1). This is what is meant by the phrase "together with Brahman."

The wise one, having become Brahman, enjoys all desires simultaneously by means of his very nature as Brahman; he does not enjoy all desires—such as those dependent on dharma and other causes, or those requiring the instruments of the eyes and so forth—successively through a transmigratory form that is a reflection produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), like the reflection of the sun in water.

How then? The meaning is that, in the manner described, he enjoys all desires simultaneously—both those dependent on causes such as merit (*dharma*) and those independent of the instruments of perception such as the eyes—by means of the eternal Brahman-self whose nature is the universal Self, which is omniscient and omnipresent. "By the wise one" (*vipaścitā*) means by the intelligent, omniscient one; that which is omniscience is his wisdom (*vaipaścitya*), and by means of that omniscient nature, he enjoys [them] through Brahman. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the mantra.

The entire meaning of the *vallī* was enunciated by the Brāhmaṇa passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*TaittU* 2.1.1). That meaning, indicated by the aphorism, has been explained in brief by the mantra. Now, since a detailed determination of its meaning must be made, the subsequent portion of the text—which serves as its exposition—is commenced, beginning with the words, "From that, indeed, from this... and so forth.

And since it was stated at the beginning of the mantra, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (TaittU 2.1.1), one might ask: how is it both true and infinite? To this he says: for in that regard, infinity is threefold—by way of space, by way of time, and by way of substance. For example, space is infinite by way of space, for there is no spatial limitation of it; yet space is not infinite by way of time, nor is it infinite by way of substance. Why? Because it is an effect (*kārya*).

Brahman does not possess finitude even with respect to time, as it is like space, because it is unproduced (*akārya*). For only a produced entity is delimited by time; and Brahman is unproduced. Therefore, it is infinite even with respect to time. Likewise, it is infinite with respect to substance (*vastu*). How, then, is there infinity with respect to substance? Because it is non-different from everything. For a distinct entity constitutes the limit of another entity; for the cognition of one entity ceases upon reaching another distinct entity.

That from which the cognition of something ceases is its limit (*anta*). For example, since the cognition of "cowness" ceases with respect to "horseness," cowness has horseness as its limit; thus, it is indeed finite. And that limit is observed in distinct entities, but there is no such differentiation in Brahman. Therefore, Brahman is infinite even in terms of its actual reality (*vastutaḥ*). But how is it said that Brahman is non-different from all things? Because it is the cause of all things. For Brahman is the cause of all things, including time, space, and so forth.

If it is argued that Brahman is actually finite with respect to its effects, we say no; for the state of being an effect is unreal. Indeed, apart from the cause, there is no such thing as an "effect" that exists in reality from which the cognition of the cause could be withdrawn. As another Śruti states: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth" (ChU 6.4.1), and likewise, "Being alone is the truth. Therefore, because it is the cause of space and the rest, Brahman is infinite in terms of space.

For it is well known that space is infinite in terms of location (*deśataḥ*), and since this [Self] has that as its cause, the infinity of the Self in terms of location is established. Indeed, nothing is seen in the world arising from what is not all-pervading (*asarvagata*) to become all-pervading. Therefore, the infinity of the Self in terms of location is unsurpassed; likewise, it is unsurpassed in terms of time (*kālataḥ*) because it is unproduced (*akāryatva*), and in terms of substance (*vastutaḥ*) because there is no other distinct entity apart from it. For this very reason, it is unsurpassed reality.

The word "from that" (*tasmāt*) refers back to Brahman as formulated in the root aphorism; the word "from this" (*etasmāt*) refers to it immediately following, as characterized by the mantra-text. That Brahman which was first formulated in the Brāhmaṇa passage, and which was subsequently characterized by the statement, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma*, TaittU 2.1.1)—from that very Brahman, from the Self (*ātmanaḥ*), which is denoted by the word "Self. For the Self is indeed the source of all this, according to another scriptural passage: "That is the Truth, that is the Self" (*tatsatyaṃ sa ātmā*, ChU 6.8.16).

Therefore, Brahman is the Self. From this Brahman, which is the very nature of the Self, space (*ākāśa*) was produced—that is, it arose. Space is that which has sound as its quality and provides room for material objects. From that space, wind (*vāyu*)—possessing twice the qualities, namely its own quality of touch together with the prior quality of space, sound—was produced; the word "was produced" is understood to carry over from the previous context. And from wind, fire (*agni*) was produced, possessing three qualities: its own quality of form (color) together with the two prior qualities.

From fire, by its own quality of taste and by the three preceding qualities, water is produced as possessing four qualities. From water, by its own quality of smell and by the four preceding qualities, earth is produced as possessing five qualities. From earth come plants; from plants, food; and from food, transformed into the form of semen, comes the person (puruṣa) endowed with the shape of a head, hands, and so forth.

This person, indeed, consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*), being a modification of the essence of food; for from all the limbs [of the body], the seed—namely, the semen—is produced as a manifestation of *tejas* (vital heat) fashioned in the form of a person. Therefore, whoever is born from it must likewise be of that same human form. This is because, among all species, we observe a rule regarding the form of the progenitor in those who are born. Although all beings are equally modifications of the essence of food and equally belong to the lineage of Brahman, why is the "person" alone mentioned? It is because of its preeminence.

What, then, is this preeminence? It is the qualification for ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). For it is the person alone who, being capable, desirous, and not excluded, is qualified for the purpose of ritual action and knowledge—being one who is both seeker and wise. Regarding the person, indeed, the Self is more fully manifest; for he is most perfectly endowed with wisdom: "He speaks what is known, he sees what is known, he knows what is to come, he perceives the worlds and the non-worlds, and through his mortality, he beholds immortality"—thus is he endowed.

For we see in other scriptural passages such as, "Now, for the other animals, hunger and thirst alone constitute their cognition" (AitĀ 2.3.2–5). Indeed, it is this person who is intended here to be led by means of knowledge to the innermost Brahman; yet, since his intellect has been habituated to identifying with external forms that are not the Self, it is impossible to suddenly make it turn toward the innermost inward Self—which is without support—without some specific point of reference. Therefore, [the text proceeds] by means of the conceptualization of a similarity between the perceived body and the Self.

Introducing [the topic] by means of the illustration of the moon and its branches, he says: "Of him, this indeed is the head. Of this very person consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*), this is the well-known head. Since in the cases of the one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) and the others, no head is seen, the phrase "this indeed is the head" is stated here so that the same [misconception] might not arise. The application [of the analogy] is to be understood in the same way for the wings and so forth. This right arm of the one facing east is the right wing; this left arm is the northern wing.

This middle portion of the body is the self (*ātman*), for the scripture states: "The self is indeed the center of these limbs" (AitU 3.5.4). That limb which is below the navel is the tail, the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). It is called the foundation because one stands firm by means of it. It is called a "tail" because of the common characteristic of hanging downwards, just as the tail of a cow. Having established this with reference to the physical body, the status of the subsequent sheaths—beginning with that consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*)—as figurative forms is established, like a statue cast from molten copper poured into a mold.

Regarding this, there is also the following verse: with reference to that very same meaning expressed in the Brāhmaṇa which elucidates the self consisting of food (annamaya-ātman), there is this verse, a mantra.
Thus ends the first section (anuvāka). 1.

From food indeed are creatures born, whatever dwell upon the earth; moreover, by food alone they live, and into it they finally pass away. For food is the eldest of beings; therefore it is called the "all-remedy. Verily, all food comes to those who worship food as Brahman. For food is the eldest of beings; therefore it is called the "all-remedy. From food beings are born; once born, they grow by food. It is eaten, and it eats beings.

Therefore it is called food. Now, different from this self consisting of the essence of food is another inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). By that [self] this one is filled. That very self is indeed of the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*). Following its person-like form, this [self] is person-like. Of that [self], the out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the head; the diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the right wing; the downward breath (*apāna*) is the left wing; space is the trunk; and the earth is the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse: [The verse follows.]
Thus ends the second section.

From food, having been transformed into the state of sap and so forth—*vā* is for the purpose of recollection—the creatures (*prajāḥ*), both stationary and moving, are born. Whatever beings there are, undistinguished [by class], that take refuge in the earth, that is, those who depend upon the earth, all of them are born from food alone. Moreover (*atho*), once born, they live by food alone; the meaning is that they sustain their vital breaths and grow. Furthermore, they also *apiyanti*, that is, they go back into (*apigacchanti*) that very food. The word *api* has the sense of the word *prati*; the meaning is that they dissolve back into food.

"In the end" means at the conclusion of life, characterized by its final activity. Why? Because food (*anna*) is the "eldest," meaning the first-born, of living beings (*bhūta*, i.e., sentient creatures). For food is the cause of all other beings, such as those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth; therefore, all progeny originate from food, live by food, and dissolve into food. And because it is thus, food is called the "panacea" (*sarvauṣadha*), for it pacifies the burning of the bodies of all living beings.

The fruit for those who know food as Brahman is now stated: they indeed obtain all that is born of food in its entirety. Who are they? Those who meditate upon food as Brahman, as previously described. How? [Thinking: "I am born of food, my self is food, and my dissolution is in food; therefore, food is Brahman. But why does meditation on the Self as food result in the fruit of obtaining all food? It is said: "For food is the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*) among beings. Because it was produced before the other beings, it is the eldest; and because it is the eldest, it is called the "all-healing herb" (*sarvauṣadha*).

Therefore, for one who meditates upon the Self as all food, the attainment of all food is logically established. The statement, "From food beings are born; once born, they grow by food," is repeated for the purpose of providing a conclusion. Now, the etymological definition of food (*anna*) is stated: "That which is eaten and enjoyed by beings, and which itself eats and consumes beings—for that reason, because it is consumed by beings and because it is the consumer of beings, it is called food (*anna*). The word *iti* marks the completion of the first sheath (*kośa*).

Desiring to show, through knowledge, that Brahman is the innermost of all selves beginning with the one consisting of food and ending with the one consisting of bliss—by removing the five sheaths created by ignorance, just as one removes the husks from many-branched kodrava grain to reveal the rice within—the scripture introduces it with the words, "From this very one, which consists of food," and so forth.

Therefore, distinct from and internal to this aforementioned body composed of the essence of food, there is another inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). Like the physical body, it is falsely imagined as the self; "breath" (*prāṇa*) is wind, and that which consists of it is "composed of breath" (*tanmaya*), meaning it is primarily made up of it. This body composed of the essence of food is filled by that body composed of breath, just as a leather bag is filled with air. Indeed, this self composed of breath is also shaped like a person (*puruṣavidha*), having the form of a person with a head, wings, and so forth. Is this due to its own nature? No, he says:

It is well known, first of all, that the self consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) has the form of a person. Following the person-like nature—that is, the human shape—of that self consisting of the essence of food, the self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) also becomes person-like; it is not so by its own nature, but like a cast image in a mold. In this way, each preceding one has the form of a person, and following that, each subsequent one becomes person-like; furthermore, each preceding one is filled by each subsequent one.

How, then, is its anthropomorphic form explained? Of that *prāṇamaya*—which is a modification of air—the *prāṇa* itself is the head; that is, the specific function (*vṛtti*) of the *prāṇa* which issues from the mouth and nostrils is figuratively conceived as the head, because of the scriptural statement. In every case, the conception of the wings and other parts arises solely from the scriptural statement. The *vyāna*, the function of the *vyāna*, is the right wing. The *apāna* is the left wing.

Space is the self (*ātman*). That specific function (*vṛttiviśeṣa*) residing in space, which is called "the equal" (*samāna*), is the self; it is the self because, within the context of the functions of breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), it stands in the middle and thus relates to the other peripheral functions as their center. For the status of being the self belongs to that which stands in the middle, as is well known from the Vedic scripture: "The self is the center of these limbs" (AitU 3.5.4). Earth is the tail, the support. By "earth" is meant the deity Earth, who is the sustainer of the internal breath (*ādhyātmika-prāṇa*) because she is the cause of its stability.

"For this very [earth] supports the downward breath of a person," so says another scriptural passage. Otherwise, due to its weight, the body would either move upward through the function of the *udāna* breath or fall down. Therefore, the earth-deity is the tail, the support of the self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). With reference to that very same matter concerning the self consisting of breath, there is this verse:

The gods breathe after the *prāṇa*; so do humans and animals. For *prāṇa* is the life-span (*āyus*) of beings; therefore it is called "the whole life-span. Those who meditate upon *prāṇa* as Brahman attain their whole life-span. For *prāṇa* is the life-span of beings; therefore it is called "the whole life-span. This is indeed its embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*), which belongs to the former [sheath]. Now, different from this *prāṇamaya* is another inner self, consisting of mind (*manomaya*). By that, this [sheath] is filled.

Verily, this [Brahman] is indeed of the form of a person. Following its person-like form, [the individual] is of the form of a person. Of that [Brahman], the Yajus is the head; the Ṛk is the right wing; the Sāman is the left wing; the Instruction (Ādeśa) is the body; and the Atharvāṅgirases are the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the third section.

"The gods breathe after breath. The gods, beginning with Agni, breathe after breath—that is, after the wind-self, which possesses the power of breathing—having become one with it, they breathe; they perform the act of breathing and thus become possessed of activity through the action of breathing. Alternatively, because this context concerns the internal self (*adhyātma*), "the gods" refers to the sense organs; they breathe after breath, meaning they move in accordance with the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). Likewise, humans and animals also become possessed of movement only through the act of breathing.

And for this reason, living beings do not possess a self consisting of food (*annamaya*) alone as something limited. What then? Human beings and others possess a self also by means of the vital-breath consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*), which is common to all and pervades every physical body. In this same way, all living beings possess a self through the subsequent layers—beginning with that consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and so forth—which are each more pervasive than the preceding ones, increasingly subtle, ending with that consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), composed of the elements starting with space (*ākāśa*), and produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Likewise, they possess the Self through that which is innate—the eternal, unchanging, all-pervading cause of space and so forth, characterized by truth, knowledge, and infinity, which transcends the five sheaths and is the Self of all. For that indeed is the Self of all in the ultimate sense; this too is stated by implication. As for the statement, "The gods breathe after the breath," he asks why that is so and says: because the breath (*prāṇa*) is the life-force, the very living, of all beings who possess breath.

For according to another Vedic text, "As long as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) dwells in this body, so long is there life. Therefore, it is "all-life" (*sarvāyuṣam*). The life of all is "all-life" (*sarvāyuḥ*); "all-life" itself is called "all-life" (*sarvāyuṣam*). This is because death is universally known to occur upon the departure of the vital breath; for the fact that the vital breath constitutes one's entire life is well-established in the world.

Therefore, having stepped out from this external, non-common *annamaya* self, those who worship the internal, common *prāṇamaya* self as Brahman—thinking, "I am the *prāṇa*, the self of all beings, because I am the cause of life and longevity"—they attain the full span of life in this world; they do not die by premature death (*apamṛtyu*) before reaching their natural lifespan. This is the meaning. As for the phrase "a hundred years," it is more appropriate [to understand it as] "he attains the full span of life," since that is well-known from the Vedic revelation.

What is the reason? For *prāṇa* is the life-force (*āyus*) of living beings; therefore, it is called "the whole of life" (*sarvāyuṣa*). The statement beginning with "For *prāṇa*... is repeated for the purpose of establishing the cause for attaining the fruit of knowledge—that whoever meditates upon Brahman as possessing a certain quality becomes a partaker of that quality. Of that preceding *annamaya*, this very one which consists of *prāṇa* is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) existing within the *annamaya* body. Who is he? He who is this *prāṇamaya*. The rest, beginning with "From him, indeed, from this one," has already been explained. There is another inner self consisting of mind (*manomaya*).

"Mind" (*manas*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of volition and the like; that which is composed of this is "mind-made" (*manomaya*). This is the inner self (*ātman*) within the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Of this [self], the *Yajus* is indeed the head. "Yajus" is a specific type of mantra whose syllables, feet, and terminations are not fixed; the word *yajus* here denotes that class of mantra. Its status as the head is due to its preeminence. Its preeminence arises from its direct contribution (*sannipatyopakāra*) to sacrifices and other rites, for it is by means of the *Yajus*—accompanied by the utterance of *svāhā* and so forth—that the oblation is offered. Alternatively, the conceptualization of the head and other limbs is based on scriptural injunction (*vācanikī*) and applies everywhere.

For the mental modification (*vṛtti*)—which has as its objects the location, effort, intonation, sound, syllables, words, and sentences; which consists of their conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*); which is permeated by them; and which is distinguished by the convention of the *Yajus*—is called "the *Yajus*" when it proceeds through the channels of the sense organs such as the ear. Likewise for the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*. And thus, since the mantras are modifications of the mind, it is the modification itself that is repeated; therefore, mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*) is logically established. Otherwise, because it would not be an object [of the senses], the mantra could not be repeated like a jar or other external objects, and thus mental recitation would not be possible.

Furthermore, the repetition of mantras is enjoined many times in ritual acts. If it is argued that the repetition of the mantra occurs through the repetition of the memory directed toward the syllables, we say no; for the primary meaning would be impossible. In the injunction, "He recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times" (ŚB 11.2.1.4), the repetition of the *ṛc* (verse) is heard. In that context, if the *ṛc* were not the object [of the injunction] and one were instead to perform repetition by means of a memory directed toward it, then the primary meaning enjoined—the repetition of the *ṛc* expressed as "he recites the first verse three times"—would be abandoned.

Therefore, the self-consciousness—which is delimited by the limiting adjuncts of mental modifications (*manovṛtti-upādhi*), which culminates in mental modifications, which is without beginning or end, and which is denoted by the word *yajus*—is the knowledge of the Self; these are the *mantras*. In this way, the eternity of the Vedas is established. Otherwise, if they were objects [of perception], they would be non-eternal like color and other such qualities. This is not tenable.

Furthermore, the scriptural passage, "That wherein all the Vedas become one—that is the Self within the mind" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11.1), which declares the oneness of the eternal Self, would be consistent only if the *Ṛg* and other Vedas were eternal. Likewise, there is the wording of a mantra: "In this imperishable, supreme ether of the *Ṛk*, all the gods have taken their seat" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.8). Here, the term "instruction" (*ādeśa*) refers to the Brāhmaṇa, because it instructs (*ādiśati*) the specific matters that are to be taught.

The mantras seen by Atharvan and Aṅgiras, as well as the Brāhmaṇas, constitute the tail—the foundation—because they primarily consist of rites for the purpose of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), such as those for pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika). Regarding this as well, there is the following verse which reveals the Self consisting of mind, as before.

"From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—he who knows that bliss of Brahman fears nothing at any time. This is indeed the embodied self of the former; from this very one consisting of mind, there is another inner self consisting of consciousness. By that, this [former] is filled. That one, indeed, is of the form of a person. Following its person-like form, this [self] is of the form of a person. Faith is its head; truth is its right wing.
Truth is the head; Yoga is the self; the Great is the tail, the support. On this point, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the fourth section.

"From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it," and so forth. Of that preceding one, the *prāṇamaya*, this very one is the embodied self (*śārīra*); "embodied" means existing within the body consisting of *prāṇa*. Which one? This one who consists of mind (*manomaya*). From that, from this very one, and so forth, as before. There is another inner self, consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), which is internal to the one consisting of mind; the one consisting of mind has been described as the self of the Vedas.

Vijñāna is the intellect whose object is the meaning of the Vedas and which consists of certainty; it is a quality of the internal organ characterized by determination (adhyavasāya). That which has this as its essence—the self (ātman) brought about by certainties and cognitions that are themselves the nature of the means of valid knowledge—is "consisting of vijñāna" (vijñānamaya). For sacrifices and other rites are sustained by being preceded by the cognition of the means of valid knowledge; moreover, he will state in a verse that [vijñāna] is the cause of sacrifice and so forth. For in one who possesses certain cognition, faith first arises regarding the duties to be performed.

That [faith] is the head, as it were, because it is the first among all duties that must be performed. *Ṛta* and *satya* are exactly as previously explained. *Yoga* means application, concentration, or composure. It is the self (*ātman*), as it were; for when one possesses the self—that is, when one is disciplined and composed—the limbs such as faith and the rest become capable of attaining the truth, just like the limbs of a person who has a self. Therefore, concentration (*samādhāna*) or yoga is the self of that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). *Mahaḥ* (the Great) is the tail, the support. *Mahaḥ* refers to the principle of Greatness (*mahattattva*), the first-born.

[It is] "the great first-born Yakṣa" according to another Śruti passage. It is the "tail," the foundation, because it is the cause; for the cause is indeed the foundation of its effects, just as the earth is the foundation of trees and creepers. And the Great Principle (*mahattattva*) is the cause of all cognitions; therefore, that is the foundation of the Self consisting of cognition. Regarding this, there is also the following verse, as before—just as there were verses elucidating the [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa, so too there is one for the one consisting of cognition. 4.

"Consciousness performs the sacrifice; it also performs the ritual acts. All the gods worship consciousness as the supreme Brahman. If one knows consciousness to be Brahman, and if one does not become negligent regarding it, then, having cast off all evils from the body, one enjoys all desires. This very one is the embodied self (śārīra-ātman) of the former [the mind-self]; it is that which belongs to the previous one. Now, different from this self consisting of consciousness is another inner self consisting of bliss (ānanda-maya). By that [self of bliss], this [self of consciousness] is filled. And this [self of bliss] is indeed of the form of a person.

Following its human form, it is itself human in form. Its head is joy; its right wing is delight; its left wing is extreme delight; its self is bliss; and Brahman is its tail, the foundation. On this point, there is also this verse: *Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.1*
Thus ends the fifth section.

Consciousness performs the sacrifice; for it is one possessed of consciousness who performs the sacrifice preceded by faith and the like. Therefore, consciousness has the status of an agent in the sense that "it performs [the sacrifice]. And it performs the ritual acts as well. Since everything has consciousness as its agent, it is logical that the Self consisting of consciousness is Brahman.

Furthermore, Brahman is consciousness (*vijñāna*). All the gods, Indra and the rest, worship—that is, they meditate upon—Brahman as the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*), because it is the first-born, either due to its being the first-born of all things or because it precedes all activities. The meaning is that they worship by forming an identification with that Brahman which consists of consciousness. Therefore, through their worship of the Great Brahman, they become possessed of knowledge and sovereignty.

And if one knows—that is, if one understands—that this consciousness is Brahman, and does not merely know it but also does not become negligent toward that Brahman—negligence consisting in regarding external non-self-objects as the self—then, since such negligence toward the contemplation of the Self within the Brahman consisting of consciousness would be expected, its prevention is stated: "If one does not become negligent toward that."

The meaning is: if one does not remain meditating on the nature of the Self as being solely the Brahman consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), having abandoned the sense of self-identity in the [sheaths] beginning with that consisting of food (*annamaya*); then what would happen? This is stated: "having cast off all evils from the body. For all evils have their cause in the conceit of the body; and since their cause is the conceit of the Self in the Brahman consisting of consciousness, their abandonment occurs when that cause is removed, just as shadow disappears when the umbrella is removed.

Therefore, having abandoned right here in the body all evils—which arise from the body and are caused by the conceit of identifying with the body—one attains the nature of the Brahman consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*); the meaning is that one fully enjoys (i.e., experiences) all desires residing therein by means of the self consisting of consciousness itself. Of that former [self] consisting of mind (*manomaya*), this very one is the "bodily" (*śārīra*) self—that is, existing within the body which consists of mind. Which one? This very one who consists of consciousness. The phrase "from that, or from this" has its meaning already explained.

The understanding that the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is an effect-self (*kāryātman*) arises from both the context and the word *mayaṭ*. For here, the effect-selves composed of food and so forth—the elemental beings—are the subject under discussion; and this "consisting of bliss" falls within that same context. Furthermore, the suffix *mayaṭ* is seen here in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), as in the case of "consisting of food" (*annamaya*). Therefore, the "consisting of bliss" should be understood as an effect-self. Moreover, because of the transition, the text will later state: "He approaches the self consisting of bliss" (*TaittU* 2.8.5).

Furthermore, the transition of things that consist of effects is observed to occur by means of things that consist of food (*anna*). Moreover, the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is heard of in the scriptures as the object of the act of transition, as in the passage: "He transitions into the Self consisting of food. And it is not possible for there to be a transition into the Self itself; for this would contradict the context and is logically impossible. Indeed, a transition of the Self into itself is not possible, because there is no distinction within the Self. Furthermore, Brahman is the very nature of the one who transitions, and thus the conceptualization of [Brahman] having a head and so forth is untenable.

For indeed, the metaphorical attribution of limbs such as the head and so forth is not possible in a cause such as space (*ākāśa*), which possesses the characteristics already described and does not fall within the category of an effect; this is because of scriptural passages that negate specific attributes, such as "invisible, bodiless, unspoken, without abode" (TaittU 2.7.1), "neither gross nor subtle" (BĀU 3.8.8), and "the Self is 'not this, not this'" (BĀU 3.9.26), as well as because the citation of a mantra [in that context] would be untenable.

For there can be no suspicion that Brahman does not exist within the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), which is perceived through direct experience as characterized by limbs such as "joy as its head"; thus, the citation of the mantra, "He becomes non-existent, if he knows Brahman as non-existent" (TaittU 2.6.1), is appropriate [only if the *ānandamaya* is not the Supreme]. Furthermore, the statement "Brahman is the tail, the support" would also be untenable if Brahman were grasped separately as a mere support. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is indeed included within the realm of effects (*kārya*), and is not the Supreme Self itself.

"Ānanda" is the fruit of knowledge and action; that which consists of this fruit is "ānandamaya. And it is more internal than the "vijñānamaya," because scripture declares its greater internality compared to the "vijñānamaya," which has sacrifice and so forth as its cause. For the fruit of knowledge and action must be most internal, since it exists for the sake of the enjoyer. Moreover, the self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is more internal than the preceding ones, because knowledge and action are for the sake of pleasure and the like; indeed, knowledge and action are prompted by pleasure and its kind.

Therefore, it is logically consistent that the nature of pleasure and so forth—which are of the form of fruits—is more internal than the *vijñānamaya* (the layer consisting of consciousness) because of its proximity to the Self; for the *ānandamaya* (the layer consisting of bliss), which is produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of pleasure and so forth, is perceived in dreams as resting upon the *vijñānamaya*. Of that *ānandamaya* Self, "pleasure" (*priya*)—born from the sight of a beloved son or similar object—is the "head," because of its primacy, just as the head is the foremost part of the body. "Joy" (*moda*) is the exhilaration caused by the attainment of what is pleasant. And that same exhilaration, when intensified, is "great joy" (*pramoda*).

"Ānanda" (bliss) is the commonality of happiness; it is the Self because it is woven through all the "pleasurable" components such as beloved ones and the like. "Ānanda" is the Supreme Brahman. For that [Brahman] is manifested when the specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*)—which is presented by virtuous action and conditioned by specific objects such as son, friend, and so forth—is clear and not obscured by darkness (*tamas*). This is what is well known in the world as "the pleasure derived from an object."

Because the karma that brings about specific modifications of that [internal organ] is unstable, pleasure is momentary. Thus, to the extent that the internal organ attains purity through austerity that destroys darkness, through knowledge, celibacy, and faith, to that same extent, as the internal organ becomes isolated and serene, a particular bliss is elevated and expands. And it will be said: "He is indeed the essence (rasa); for having obtained this very essence, one becomes joyful..."

For it is said in another Vedic text: "He alone causes bliss" (TaittU 2.7.1), and "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss" (BĀU 4.3.32). And thus, with respect to the progressive cessation of desire, the excellence of bliss will be described as increasing a hundredfold at each successive stage.

And thus, for this Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) which has been progressively elevated, with respect to the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman—which is the very Brahman under discussion, characterized as truth, knowledge, and infinity, for the sake of whose realization the five sheaths consisting of food and so forth were introduced, and which is interior to them all, by which they all possess a self—that Brahman is the tail, the foundation.

And that very non-dual Brahman, which is the ultimate limit of all duality imagined through ignorance, is the foundation; for it is the culminating point of the unity of that which consists of bliss. That one non-dual Brahman, which is the ultimate limit of the duality imagined through ignorance, exists as the foundation and the tail. Regarding this very matter, there is this verse:

"If one knows Brahman as non-existent, he himself becomes non-existent; but if one knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing. This very one is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of the former [the person within the sun]. Now, therefore, follow these further questions: Does anyone who is ignorant go to that world after departing? Or does anyone who is wise, after departing, attain that world? He desired: "May I become many, may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity...

It created all this, whatever exists here. Having created it, It entered into that very thing. Having entered it, It became the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*); the defined (*nirukta*) and the undefined (*anirukta*); the supported (*nilayana*) and the unsupported (*anilayana*); consciousness (*vijñāna*) and non-consciousness (*avijñāna*); truth (*satya*) and falsehood (*anṛta*). Whatever exists here is truth; they call it "Truth. Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the sixth section.

It is indeed non-existent, just like that which is non-existent; for just as that which is non-existent has no connection with human goals (*puruṣārtha*), so too does that [Brahman] become unconnected with human goals. Which one is this? It is he who, if he should know—that is, discern—that Brahman is non-existent and not present. Conversely, if he should know that Brahman exists—even though it is the locus of all conceptual constructions, the seed of all activity, and that in which all distinctions have subsided—then why, one might ask, would there be any doubt regarding its non-existence? We reply: because Brahman transcends all empirical discourse (*vyavahāra*).

For when the intellect is conditioned by the existence of things that are mere verbal designations within the sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), it likewise apprehends non-existence in their opposite—that which transcends worldly transaction. Just as it is well known that a jar or the like, being established as an object of worldly transaction, is "existent," while its opposite is "non-existent," so too, by analogy with that, there might arise a suspicion regarding the non-existence of Brahman here as well. Therefore, it is said: "If one knows that 'Brahman exists'..."

What, then, would happen for one who knows that "it exists"? To this he says: the knowers of Brahman recognize such a person—who is existent (*santam*), present, having attained the nature of the Self which is ultimately real by way of the essence of Brahman—as one who knows Brahman. Therefore, from that knowledge of its existence, the meaning is that he becomes to others as one whose nature is to be known as Brahman.

Alternatively, he who thinks "Brahman does not exist" arrives at the non-existence of the entire path of the righteous, characterized by the system of castes, stages of life, and so forth, because of his lack of faith; for that [path] exists for the purpose of attaining Brahman. Therefore, such a person is called an *nāstika*—one who is non-existent and wicked—in the world.

If one knows that "Brahman exists" as being the opposite of that [non-existence], then, because he faithfully and correctly follows that true path characterized by the established order of castes, stages of life, and so forth—which is the means for attaining that Brahman—the virtuous know him to be a "good man" (sat) who stands upon the right path. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that Brahman must indeed be understood as "it exists. Of that former self consisting of knowledge (*vijñānamaya*), this very one existing in the body consisting of knowledge is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*).

Who is this? It is this one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Regarding him, there is no doubt as to his non-existence; however, because Brahman is devoid of all particularities (*viśeṣa*), a doubt concerning its non-existence is appropriate, and because Brahman is the universal commonality (*sāmānya*) of all things. Since it is so, therefore—immediately thereafter—the "subsequent questions" (*anupraśna*) of the listener, the disciple, are those questions which follow upon the teacher's statement. For Brahman is common to both the knower and the ignorant, since it is the cause of ether and the rest.

Therefore, the attainment of Brahman by even the ignorant person is suspected [as a possibility]. Or rather, does even the ignorant person—using the word *cana* in the sense of "even"—go to or attain that world, the Supreme Self, after departing from here? Or does he not go? A second question is also to be understood here, because of the plural number in the expression "subsequent questions" (*anupraśnāḥ*).

Two further questions concern the wise man: if even an ignorant person does not go to Brahman, which is the common cause, then one might suspect that even the wise man does not go to Brahman; therefore, a question is asked regarding him: "Or is it the wise man? By drawing down the syllable *u* from the word *uta* to be mentioned later and joining the syllable *ta* with the preceding word *uta*, and by prefixing the word *uta* to this *aho*, he asks: "Or is it the wise man (*utāho vidvān*)?"

"Does even some wise man, a knower of Brahman, after departing from here, attain—that is, reach—that world? [The form] *samaśnute u* being thus established, when the *ay*-substitution and the elision of *y* have been performed, there is the prolation (*pluti*) of the vowel *a*, resulting in *samaśnutā3 u*. Thus: "The wise man attains that world. Or rather, another question is: "Does even the wise man not attain it, just as the ignorant man does? Or else, there are two questions concerning the wise and the ignorant respectively.

The plural number, however, is appropriate with reference to other questions that arise by implication from the context. For it is heard in scripture: "If he knows Brahman as non-existent... if he knows Brahman as existent" (TaittU 2.6.1). Thus, there arises the doubt: "Does it exist or not? From this, the first implied question is: "Does it exist or does it not exist? Because Brahman is impartial, the second question is: "Does the ignorant one go [to Brahman] or not?

Even though Brahman is equal [to all], one might suspect that just as the ignorant one does not go, so too the knower does not go; thus, the third implied question is: "Does the knower attain [Brahman] or does he not attain it?"

To provide an answer to these [objections], the subsequent portion of the text is commenced. Therein, first of all, existence (*astitva*) itself is stated. Regarding that which was said, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (*TaittU* 2.1.1), it must be explained how its truthfulness (*satyatva*) consists; this is what is now stated. By the very mention of existence (*sattva*), truthfulness is expressed. For it has been said that "only Being (*sat*) is Truth. Therefore, by the very mention of existence, truthfulness is expressed.

How is this meaning understood from the text? From the sequence of the words; for the subsequent sentences are connected with this very same meaning: "They call that Truth" (TaittU 2.6.1), "If this bliss did not exist in the ether" (TaittU 2.7.1), and so forth. In this regard, it might be suspected that Brahman is non-existent. Why? Because that which exists is perceived through its specific qualities, such as a jar and the like; whereas that which does not exist is not perceived, such as a hare's horn and the like.

In that way, Brahman is not perceived; therefore, because it is not apprehended in its specific form, some claim it does not exist. That is not so. Because Brahman is the cause of space and the rest, Brahman does not not exist. Why? For all effects, such as space and the rest, are perceived as having been born from Brahman. And in the world, it is observed that whatever is born must have an existent cause, just as clay and seeds are the causes of jars, sprouts, and so forth. Therefore, because it is the cause of space and the rest, Brahman exists. Furthermore, no effect is ever perceived in the world that has been produced from what is non-existent.

If the effects such as name and form were non-existent, they would not be perceived because of their lack of self-nature; yet they are indeed perceived. Therefore, Brahman exists. Furthermore, if the effect were non-existent, even when it is apprehended, it would be permeated by non-existence; but this is not the case. Therefore, Brahman exists. In this regard, another scriptural passage explains through reasoning that the birth of the existent from the non-existent is impossible, asking, "How could the existent be born from the non-existent? Therefore, it is logical that Brahman is indeed existent.

If it were a cause like clay, seed, and so forth, then it would be insentient; but this is not so, because it possesses desire (*kāmayitṛtva*). For in the world, nothing that desires is insentient. Indeed, we have stated that Brahman is omniscient; therefore, its possession of desire is logically established. If it is argued that, because it possesses desire, it must have unfulfilled desires like those of ourselves and others, we say no, because of its sovereignty. Desires do not impel Brahman in the same way that defects such as desire impel others by bringing them under their control.

How, then, is it so? Because they are characterized by the knowledge of truth and are of the nature of its own self, they are pure; Brahman is not set in motion by them. Rather, Brahman is their impeller with regard to the karma of living beings. Therefore, Brahman possesses independence regarding desires; hence, Brahman is not one whose desires are unfulfilled. This is also because it does not depend on any other means.

Furthermore, unlike other things for which desires depend on external signs such as non-self-existent objects (dharma) and so forth, and which depend on other means consisting of instruments and effects distinct from their own selves, Brahman does not depend on such signs and the like. Rather, [desires] are non-different from its own self. This is what the text says: "He desired. That Self, from which space was produced, desired—that is, He willed. How? "May I be many; may I become abundant and manifold."

How can there be multiplicity when one [entity] enters into other things? It is said: "I shall be born" (*prajāyeya*), meaning "I shall arise. For this becoming manifold does not have as its object something external, like the birth of a son. How then? Through the manifestation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) which reside within itself. When name-and-form, which reside within and were unmanifest, are manifested, then name-and-form are manifested by Brahman—without abandoning its own essential nature—and with space and time undivided from it, throughout all states.

This differentiation of name and form is the becoming manifold of Brahman; otherwise, it would not be possible for the partless Brahman to attain multiplicity or even limitation, just as the limitation or multiplicity of space is caused solely by other entities. Therefore, the Self becomes manifold only through that [differentiation]. For there exists no entity other than the Self—whether non-self, or distinguished by space and time, or subtle, hidden, remote, past, present, or future.

Therefore, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in all their states have Brahman as their self; yet Brahman is not identical with them. Since they do not exist at all if that [Brahman] were denied, they are said to have it as their self. And through those two limiting adjuncts (upādhi), Brahman becomes the locus of all worldly transactions, such as the knower, the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, words, and their meanings.

He, being such a desirer of the Self, performed austerity (*tapas*). "Austerity" here refers to knowledge, according to another Vedic scripture which states: "His austerity consists of knowledge" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9). For one whose desires have been fulfilled, the performance of [physical] austerity is simply impossible. Thus, he "performed that austerity" means that the Self engaged in contemplation regarding the arrangement of the world to be created and so forth.

Having reflected thus and performed austerity, he created—having brought forth—all this world, which is determined by the karma and other factors of living beings, according to its place, time, name, and form, and which is experienced by all living beings in all their various states exactly as it is perceived. Whatever this is—whatever exists without distinction—having created this world, what did he do? It is said: "He entered that very world he had created."

In this regard, the following must be considered: how did he enter? Did the creator enter by that very same self, or by another? What, first of all, is logical? Because of the hearing of the suffix *-tvā*, it is logical that the one who is the creator entered by that very same [self]. But is this not illogical, since if clay is the cause, the effect consists of that very essence? For it is the cause itself that transforms into the form of the effect.

Therefore, since the effect has already arisen even before [the cause] has entered, a subsequent re-entry of the cause as a separate entity is untenable. For there is no entry of clay into the jar apart from its transformation into the jar. If it is argued that the Self enters into the effects of name and form by way of this very nature—just as clay enters the jar in the form of powder—and that this is supported by another scriptural passage, "Having entered by means of this living self" (ChU 6.3.2), this is not correct, because Brahman is one.

However, because clay is manifold by nature and possesses parts, it is logical for clay to enter into a jar in the form of powder; this is also because there are regions within the jar where the powdered clay has not yet entered. But since the Self is one and partless, and because there is no region that has not already been pervaded, its entry is not possible. How, then, could there be entry? And yet, entry is indeed logical, because it is so stated in scripture: "It entered into that very [being]" (tad evānuprāviśat). Let it be, then, that the Self possesses parts.

If it is argued that, because [the cause] possesses parts, the entry of the individual self (jīvātman) into the effects of name and form is logical—just as the hand enters the mouth—we say no, because there is no empty space. For when [the cause] has transformed into the nature of the effect, there exists no region devoid of the self apart from the effects of name and form into which the individual self could enter. If it were to enter the cause itself, it would abandon its status as an individual self, just as a jar abandons its jar-nature upon entering the clay.

Furthermore, because of the Śruti text, "He entered into that very thing," it is not logical for there to be an entry into the cause. If it is argued that [the Self] becomes merely another effect, [we reply: "He entered into that very thing. If you claim that the effect in the form of the individual soul (jīvātman), having undergone the transformation into name and form, attains the state of yet another effect, this is not so, because of contradiction. For a pot does not become another pot; moreover, it would contradict the Śruti texts on distinction, and the Śruti texts which restate the distinction of the individual soul from the effects of name and form would be contradicted.

Furthermore, because liberation would be impossible upon falling into that [state]. For one who is being liberated from something does not fall into that very same thing; it is not as if a thief or the like, who is bound by a chain, falls into the chain itself. If it is argued that [Brahman] has transformed through the distinction between external and internal—that the very cause, Brahman, has transformed into the substratum such as the body, etc., externally, and into the supported individual self (*jīvātman*), internally—we say no. For it is not logical for that which already exists outside to "enter" [itself]. Indeed, that which is already situated within something is not said to have "entered" that very thing.

The entry [of the Self] would be an entering from outside, because the meaning of the word "entering" is observed to be such; as in the expression, "having built a house, he entered it. If it is argued that the entry is like the reflection of the sun in water and so forth, we say no; because [the Self] is undivided and formless (*amūrta*). The arising of a reflection, such as that of the sun, occurs in another place—such as water which is clear by nature—only when there is something else that is limited and possessed of form. But this is not the case for the Self, because the Self, the cause of space and the rest, is formless and all-pervading.

Furthermore, because there is no other object to serve as a substratum for a reflection at a distant location, entry like that of a reflection is not logical. If this is so, then there is no entry; yet we do not perceive any other alternative, since the scripture states, "He entered into that very thing" (TaittU 2.6.1). Scripture is the cause for the arising of knowledge regarding objects beyond the senses, yet from this statement, knowledge does not arise even for those who exert effort.

"Well then, since it is meaningless, this sentence—'Having created that, he entered into it' (TaittU 2.6.1)—must be rejected. No; for it has another purpose. Why this misplaced deliberation?
