For there is another subject intended by this sentence which must be recalled: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (TaittU 2.1.1), "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (TaittU 2.1.1), and "He who knows [It] as hidden in the cave" (TaittU 2.1.1).

And that consciousness is what is intended to be expressed and is the subject at hand. For the purpose of understanding the nature of Brahman, the entire range of effects—from space down to that which consists of food—has been presented, and the inquiry into the realization of Brahman has been commenced. In this context, the self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) was shown to be distinct from the self consisting of food (*annamaya*); within that, the self consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) were introduced, leading one into the cave of consciousness. Therein, the specific self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) was revealed.

Therefore, by means of attaining the *liṅga* consisting of supreme bliss, the Self—which culminates in the increase of bliss—is [realized]. "Brahman is the tail, the support"—being the substratum of all conceptual constructions yet itself free from conceptual construction—it is to be attained within this very cave; thus, entry into it is postulated. For Brahman is not perceived elsewhere, because it is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatvāt*). Indeed, a connection with a particularity is observed to be the cause of perception, as in the case of Rāhu’s connection with the particularities of the moon and the sun.

Thus, the connection between the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the Self is the cause for the perception of Brahman, because of the proximity [of the Self] and because the inner organ is of the nature of illumination. Just as the perception of a jar or similar objects is characterized by light, so too the perception of the Self would be characterized by the light of the cognition of the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, the phrase "hidden in the cave" refers precisely to that which is the cause of perception. However, here, with reference to its locus within that [intellect], it is said again: "Having created that, He entered into it" (TaittU 2.6.1).

That very same cause, having created this effect beginning with space, has entered into it, as it were; within the internal intellect (*buddhi*), it is perceived as possessing specific attributes such as "the seer," "the hearer," "the thinker," and "the cognizer. That indeed is its entry. Therefore, that causal Brahman exists. Because it exists, it should be perceived as "it exists. Having entered into that effect, what did it become? It became both the manifest (*sat*) and the formed (*mūrta*), and the unmanifest (*tyat*) and the formless (*amūrta*).

For the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), which are unmanifested as name and form, are manifested by the Self through the Self residing within them. And once manifested, those two denoted by the terms "formed" and "formless," being inseparable from the Self in terms of space and time, are said to have become the Self. Furthermore, there is the defined (*nirukta*) and the undefined (*anirukta*); "defined" means that which has been extracted [from its context] and, distinguished by space and time from things of similar and dissimilar classes, is designated as "this is that"; the "undefined" is the opposite of that.

The terms "defined" (*nirukta*) and "undefined" (*anirukta*) are also qualifiers of the "formed" (*mūrta*) and "formless" (*amūrta*) respectively. Just as "existent" (*sat*) and "that" (*tyat*) refer to the perceptible and the imperceptible, so too do "abode" (*nilayana*) and "non-abode" (*anilayana*). An "abode"—meaning a nest or a support—is a property belonging exclusively to the formed; "non-abode," being its opposite, is a property belonging exclusively to the formless. Although "that," "undefined," and "non-abode" are properties of the formless, they nevertheless pertain only to the realm of the manifested (*vyākṛta*), because they are heard of as existing subsequent to the process of creation.

"That" (*tyad*) refers to that which is unmanifested, such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and it is also the "abodeless" (*anilayana*). Therefore, these qualifiers—being formless—refer exclusively to the realm of the manifested. "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is the sentient; "unconsciousness" (*avijñāna*) is that which is devoid of it, such as insentient stones and the like. And "truth" (*satya*) here refers to the conventional realm because of the context, not the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); for Brahman alone is the ultimate truth. Here, however, "truth" is relative to the conventional realm: water and so forth are called "true" in comparison to what is unreal, such as a mirage.

And the false is the opposite of that. What, then, was all this? It is truth, the ultimate truth; and what is that? Brahman—because it has been stated in the context that "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite."

Since this entire collection of modifications—consisting of the class of things denoted by "Being" (sat) and so forth, whether formed or formless—is without distinction, and because all this has become the one Brahman denotable by the word "Being," since there is no existence apart from that Brahman for the modifications of name and form, therefore the knowers of Brahman call that Brahman "Truth" (satyam). The question "Does it exist or does it not exist? was previously introduced; regarding the answer to that, it has been stated: "The Self desired, 'May I be many.'"

Having created, according to its will, the effects such as space and so forth—characterized by being (*sat*), truth (*tyad*), and so on—that [Brahman] entered into them, and having become manifold by seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing, it came to be much. Therefore, one should understand that this very cause of space and the rest, residing within the effect and deposited in the supreme heaven—the cave of the heart—is perceived through the specific manifestation of its own cognition; thus it is said: "It exists. With regard to this meaning expressed in the Brāhmaṇa, there is this verse, which is a mantra:

Just as in the preceding [sections], there are five mantras that reveal the Self consisting of food and so forth, even so, there is also a mantra that reveals the existence of the innermost Self by means of its effects.
Thus ends the sixth section.

"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent. From that, indeed, the existent was born. That made itself by itself; therefore, it is called well-made (*sukṛta*). What is indeed that which is well-made? It is essence (*rasa*). For only by attaining essence does one become blissful. For who indeed could inhale or exhale, if this bliss did not exist in the ether? He alone causes bliss. For when one finds fearless support in that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and without abode—then [one is truly secure]."

Then he becomes free from fear. For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Brahman], then fear comes upon him; for that very [difference] is the cause of fear for the one who knows but does not reflect. On this point there is also this verse:
Thus ends the seventh section.

"In the beginning, this was indeed non-being (*asat*). By "non-being," the unevolved Brahman is meant, which is the opposite in nature to the evolved distinctions of name and form; it does not mean absolute non-existence, for there can be no birth of being from non-being. "This"—the world differentiated by specific names and forms—was in the beginning, prior to its production, nothing but Brahman denoted by the word "non-being. From that non-being, being was born; that is, that which possesses the evolved distinctions of name and form was produced.

Is there any effect distinct from that [Brahman], as a son is distinct from his father? No, he says. That which is denoted by the word "non-existent" (asat) made itself—that is, it made its very own self. Because it is thus, that Brahman alone is called "well-made" (*sukṛta*), being the agent of its own making. It is well known in the world that Brahman is the self-acting agent because it is the cause of all things. Or, because it made everything by itself through its entire essence, therefore that very Brahman, even in its form as merit (*puṇya*), is called the cause that is "well-made."

In every respect, however, that which is denoted by the word *sukṛta* (well-done) is well-known in the world as the cause for the attainment of results and so forth—whether it be merit (*puṇya*) or something else. That common consensus is possible only if there exists an eternal, intelligent cause; therefore, that Brahman exists, because of the well-known existence of *sukṛta*. For this reason also it exists: why? Because of its being essence (*rasa*). From what [source] is the well-known status of Brahman as essence derived? To this he says: "That which is indeed *sukṛta*, that is indeed essence."

What is called *rasa* (taste/flavor) is well-known in the world as that which causes satisfaction and produces bliss, such as sweet, sour, and so forth. For having obtained—that is, attained—*rasa* itself, this person becomes blissful and happy. In the world, that which is non-existent is never seen to be a cause of bliss. Even learned Brahmins who are free from desire and devoid of longing, though lacking external means for happiness, are seen to be full of bliss as if they had obtained external *rasa*. Surely, for them, Brahman alone is that *rasa*. Therefore, that Blissful Brahman, like *rasa*, exists as the cause of their bliss. And for this reason as well:

Why? Because activities such as breathing are observed. For this body, while alive, breathes out by means of the out-breath (*apāna*) and breathes in by means of the in-breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, the movements pertaining to the wind and the senses are seen to be accomplished by the combined causes and effects. And this combination, which functions for a single purpose, is not possible without a conscious, non-composite entity, because it is not observed otherwise.

Regarding this, he says: "If this bliss were not deposited in the ether, in the supreme space, in the cave of the heart, who indeed in this world would breathe in or breathe out? This is the meaning: who would perform the act of breathing? Therefore, that Brahman exists, for the purpose of which there are activities such as the movement of the cause—the breath—and it is by that alone that the world possesses bliss. Why is this so? Because this very Supreme Self causes bliss, causes happiness, and gladdens the world according to its merit.

The meaning is this: that very Self, whose nature is bliss, is perceived by living beings as if divided due to ignorance. That Brahman exists for both the knower and the ignorant, because it is the cause of fearlessness and fear respectively. For fearlessness arises by taking refuge in a real entity (sadvastu); the cessation of fear is not possible by taking refuge in an unreal entity (asadvastu).

How is it said that this is the cause of fearlessness? It is because, when this practitioner [realizes] this Brahman—characterized as what? As "invisible" (*adṛśya*); for "visible" (*dṛśya*) means that which is to be seen, namely a modification (*vikāra*), since a modification exists for the purpose of being seen. "Invisible" means not visible, i.e., without modification. In this invisible, unmodified, non-objective state, which is "bodiless" (*anātmya*)—meaning without a body—and because it is invisible, it is therefore "without self" (*anātmya*); and because it is without self, it is therefore "indefinable" (*anirukta*). For a specific distinction is defined.

A particularity (*viśeṣa*) is a modification (*vikāra*), and Brahman is without modification because it is the cause of all modifications. Therefore, it is "indescribable" (*anirukta*). Because it is thus, it is "without abode" (*anilayana*); "abode" (*nilayana*) means a nest, a support; that which is not an abode is "without abode," meaning it is without a substratum. The meaning of the sentence is: "in this very [Brahman]—which is invisible, bodiless, indescribable, without abode, and distinct from the attributes of all effects—in this Brahman. The term "fearless" (*abhayam*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.

Or, the word "abhayām" (fearless) is transformed into another gender [to agree with "pratiṣṭhām"]. He finds—that is, he obtains—*pratiṣṭhām*, which means stability or his own essential nature (*ātmabhāva*). Then, at that time, because he no longer perceives that ignorance which is the cause of fear regarding transmigration, he becomes one who has attained fearlessness. For when he is established in his own true nature, then he sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and cognizes nothing else. Indeed, fear arises from something other than oneself; it is not logical for there to be fear of oneself by oneself.

Therefore, the Self alone is the cause of fearlessness for the Self. For Brahmins are seen to be entirely fearless even when causes of fear are present; and that would be impossible if Brahman, the protector from fear, did not exist. Thus, because they are observed to possess fearlessness, there exists that Brahman which is the cause of their fearlessness. When does the practitioner become one who has attained fearlessness? The intention is: when he sees nothing else and does not perceive any internal difference within the Self, then he has attained fearlessness.

Furthermore, when in the state of ignorance (*avidyā*), because this ignorant person perceives—due to ignorance—an object presented by ignorance like a second moon seen by one with ophthalmia, he perceives even a slight (*aram*) interval, a small gap (*chidram*), a distinction within this very Self, which is Brahman. For "perceiving a distinction" (*bhedadarśanam*) is precisely what constitutes the creation of an interval; the meaning is that he perceives even a slight difference. Then, from that cause, namely the perception of distinction, fear arises for this Self who perceives distinctions.

Therefore, for the ignorant person, the self itself is the cause of fear for the self. This is what [the text] says: "That very Brahman is the cause of fear for the ignorant one who perceives duality. For one who perceives duality—who knows, "The Lord is other than me; I am other than He; He is the transmigrating being"—fear arises for that very Brahman known as the Lord, provided he makes even a slight distinction between them. This is so for one who does not contemplate [Brahman] as oneness. Therefore, even though he is called "learned," he is truly ignorant who does not perceive the single, undivided reality of the Self.

For fear arises regarding that which is considered subject to annihilation only from the perception of a cause for annihilation; indeed, the cause of annihilation is itself not subject to annihilation. In that case, it is logical that fear—which is the effect of perceiving that [cause]—should exist toward the cause of annihilation, even though that cause is itself not subject to annihilation. Furthermore, the entire world is seen to be possessed of fear. Therefore, from the observation of fear in the world, it is understood that there must certainly exist a cause of fear, a cause of annihilation whose nature is itself not subject to annihilation, from which the world fears. On this point as well, there is this verse: [Verse follows]
Thus ends the seventh section.

"From fear of him the wind blows; from fear of him the sun rises; from fear of him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on. This is the inquiry into bliss. Suppose there were a young man, a youth, a scholar, most swift, most firm, and most strong; and suppose this entire earth were filled with his wealth. That is one human bliss. A hundred such human blisses... [equal one bliss of the Gandharvas].

That, Ānanda, is one unit of bliss for the human *gandharvas* and for a learned *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire. A hundred units of bliss for the human *gandharvas* constitute one unit of bliss for the divine *gandharvas* and for a learned *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire. A hundred units of bliss for the divine *gandharvas* constitute one unit of bliss for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) who dwell in the long-lasting world and for a learned *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire.
A hundred units of bliss for those ancestors who dwell in the long-lasting world constitute one unit of bliss for the gods born of themselves (*ājānajāḥ*).

And [the bliss] of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of those gods born of noble birth (*ājānajā*) is equal to one bliss of the gods who are deities by action (*karmadeva*), who attain godhood through their ritual acts; and [the bliss] of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of those gods who are deities by action is equal to one bliss of the gods; and [the bliss] of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of the gods is equal to one bliss of Indra.

And [the bliss] of a Vedic scholar who is not overcome by desire; a hundred such joys of Indra are equal to one joy of Bṛhaspati, and of a Vedic scholar who is not overcome by desire; a hundred such joys of Bṛhaspati are equal to one joy of Prajāpati, and of a Vedic scholar who is not overcome by desire; a hundred such joys of Prajāpati are equal to one joy of Brahman, and of a Vedic scholar who is not overcome by desire.

"Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises; out of fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, hasten along. For the wind and the others, though they are themselves powerful lords, proceed with regularity in their respective functions—such as blowing—which involve great exertion. This is appropriate only if there exists a ruler; since their activity proceeds according to fixed laws, there must exist a cause of fear for them, namely Brahman, their ruler.

Since those [beings] proceed out of fear of this Brahman, like servants of a king, and that cause of fear is blissful Brahman (*ānandaṃ brahma*), there follows this investigation (*mīmāṃsā*)—that is, a deliberation—concerning this blissful Brahman. What is to be investigated regarding bliss? It is said: Is bliss produced by the connection between an object and a subject, like worldly bliss, or is it inherent (*svābhāvika*)? Such is this investigation of bliss.

In this context, worldly bliss (*laukika-ānanda*) is the most excellent, being caused by the perfection of external and internal means; it is that which is pointed out here for the purpose of following after the bliss of Brahmā (*brahmānanda*). For, by means of this well-known bliss, the bliss accessible to one whose cognition has turned away from sense objects can be followed.

Even worldly bliss (*laukika-ānanda*) is merely a portion of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*); it becomes "worldly" when consciousness is obscured by ignorance and that ignorance is increasing, being manifested in the world by Brahmā and others through the power of karma, according to their respective cognitions, and due to their connection with the means of objects and so forth, and thus remaining unstable in the world.

That very bliss is manifested—through the removal of ignorance, desire, and karma—as the direct perception of learned *śrotriya*s whose desires are not overcome, across progressively higher levels beginning with human *gandharvas*, increasing by a hundredfold at each successive stage up to the bliss of Brahmā, the Golden Womb (*Hiraṇyagarbha*). However, when the distinction between object and subject created by ignorance is set aside through knowledge, there remains the natural, perfect, one, non-dual bliss. Desiring to illustrate this point, the text says: "A youth, in the first stage of life..."

"Sādhuyuvā" means one who is both virtuous (*sādhu*) and young (*yuvan*); this is an epithet of the youth. Since there may be a youth who is not virtuous, or a virtuous person who is not young, the qualification "virtuous and young" is necessary. An *adhyāyaka* is one who has studied the Vedas. *Āśiṣṭha* means most skilled in instructing. *Dṛḍhiṣṭha* means most firm. *Baliṣṭha* means most powerful. Thus, he is endowed with internal spiritual means.

This entire vast earth belongs to him, fully endowed with wealth—meaning that the king is the lord of the earth—both by means of wealth as an instrument of enjoyment for visible purposes, and by means of the instruments of ritual action for invisible purposes. And whatever joy he has, that is one human joy, the most excellent single joy among humans. A hundred such human joys constitute one joy of the human *gandharvas*. The joy of the human *gandharvas* is a hundred times superior to human joy.

Being human, those who have attained the state of a *gandharva* through the excellence of their karma and knowledge are called human *gandharvas*. For they are endowed with powers such as invisibility and possess subtle bodies and instruments. Consequently, they experience little resistance; they possess the power to withstand the impact of dualities and are perfected in their means of accomplishment. Thus, for a human *gandharva* who is unimpeded and capable of providing counter-measures, there arises clarity of mind (*cittaprasāda*). From that specific clarity, a specific excellence of happiness is manifested.

Thus, as one proceeds from each preceding stage to each succeeding stage, an increase in bliss by a hundredfold occurs due to the excellence of faith. However, the mention of "one who is not overcome by desire" at the outset is for the purpose of stating that the increase in bliss by a hundredfold for a learned *śrotriya* who is not struck down by desire for the enjoyment of human objects is equal to the bliss of a human *gandharva*. In the phrase "the virtuous, young student," the terms "learned" (*śrotriya*) and "free from blemish" (*avṛjina*) are understood.

For those [pleasures] are indeed indistinguishable everywhere; however, the state of being "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahatatva*) is distinguished according to the excellence or inferiority of the objects, which results in the excellence or inferiority of the pleasure. Therefore, the mention of "unassailed by desire" is for the purpose of showing the various means for attaining supreme bliss, since it is observed that through its specific degrees there is a hundredfold increase in pleasure. The rest has been explained. "The gods and Gandharvas" refers to their very birth. "Of those who dwell in the world of the long-lived" (*ciralokalokānām*) is an epithet of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).

Those ancestors whose world (*loka*) endures for a long time are called *ciralokaloka*. "Ājāna" refers to the world of the gods; those born in that *ājāna* are the *ājānajā* gods, who are born in divine abodes through the excellence of their *smārta* (tradition-based) rites. The *karma-devas* are those who reach even the status of gods solely through Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra*. The "gods" (*deva*) here refers to the thirty-three *havirbhuj* (sacrificial-eaters); Indra is their lord, and Bṛhaspati is his preceptor (*ācārya*).

Prajāpati is Virāj, whose body is the three worlds, Brahmā, who is both the aggregate and the individual, pervading the entire sphere of transmigratory existence. Therein these various distinctions of bliss attain unity; there, too, is the Dharma caused by that, the knowledge having that as its object, and unsurpassed freedom from being overcome by desire. This very Hiraṇyagarbha is Brahmā, and this is his bliss, which is perceived directly in every way by one who is learned in the Vedas, free from crookedness, and not overcome by desire.

Therefore, it is understood that these three are the means [to the realization of Brahman]. Among them, being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) and being free from crookedness (*avṛjinatva*) are constant requirements, whereas being unhindered by desire (*akāmahatatva*) is what is enhanced; thus, its status as an excellent means is understood. And through the excellence of this state of being unhindered by desire, the bliss of Brahman—which is directly perceived by the learned (*śrotriya*)—is apprehended as being but a single fraction (*mātrā*) of that supreme bliss. This is known from another scriptural passage: "On this very bliss, other beings live by depending on a mere fraction" (BĀU 4.3.32).

This very bliss is that of which all other measures of bliss are like scattered droplets from the waters of the ocean; where they have attained oneness, that is this supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), because it is natural non-duality (*advaitatva*). Here, there is no distinction between bliss and the one who experiences bliss.

That which is here in this person and that which is there in the sun are one. He who knows this, departing from this world, passes into this self consisting of food, passes into this self consisting of vital breath, passes into this self consisting of mind, passes into this self consisting of consciousness, and passes into this self consisting of bliss. Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the eighth section.

This result of the inquiry is now summarized: "He who is this person" (sa yaścāyaṃ puruṣaḥ). He who is hidden in the cave, having created the effects beginning with space and ending with that which consists of food (*annamaya*), and having entered into that very [creation], is pointed out by the words "he who. Who is he? This person within the body.

That which is in the sun—that supreme bliss directly perceived by the one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), of which the elements beginning with Brahmā, who are worthy of happiness, subsist upon a single portion—it is that very thing which is pointed out as "that which is in the sun. It is one, just as the space within a jar situated in a different location is one with the [great] space. Now, an objection: in pointing that out, the reference "that which is this in the person" (*sa yaś cāyaṃ puruṣe*) is not appropriate for the internal self (*adhyātma*) without qualification; rather, "that which is this in the right eye" (*yaś cāyaṃ dakṣiṇe 'kṣan*) would be appropriate, because of its well-known status.

No, because the Supreme Self is the subject under discussion. For the Supreme Self alone is the subject in the passages: "In the unseen, the bodiless" (TaittU 2.7.1), "From fear of it the wind blows" (TaittU 2.8.1), and "This is the inquiry into bliss" (TaittU 2.8.1). Indeed, it is not proper to mention something that is neither the subject nor previously introduced; moreover, the knowledge of the Supreme Self is what is intended to be taught. Therefore, it is the Supreme Self alone that is indicated by the words "He is one. [Objection: But the inquiry into bliss was the subject at hand, and its result must also be concluded.

Inseparable, innate bliss is the Supreme Self alone; it is not produced by the relationship between an object and a subject. But is this not a description consistent with that [teaching], since [the Taittirīya Upaniṣad] says, "That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun, they are one," thus sublatting the distinctions residing in different loci? But even so, is not the mention of the specific quality of the sun purposeless? It is not purposeless, for its purpose is to eliminate [any notion of] superiority or inferiority.

For if that supreme excellence of duality—characterized by the formed and the formless—which resides within the sun, becomes equal when the distinctions pertaining to the person are obliterated in comparison to supreme bliss, then for one who has attained that state there is neither any superiority nor inferiority; thus it is appropriate that [the scripture] says, "He finds the fearless foundation" (TaittU 2.7.1). The further inquiry as to whether [Brahman] exists or does not exist has been explained.

On account of the attainment of effects, the acquisition of rasa, the animation of life, the establishment of fearlessness, and the perception of fear, that cause—Brahman, consisting of space and so forth—certainly exists; thus, one preliminary question has been resolved. There remain two other preliminary questions concerning the attainment and non-attainment of Brahman by the knower and the ignorant respectively. Among these, the final question is whether the knower partakes [of Brahman] or does not partake. To resolve that, it is said. Since the middle question is resolved by the very resolution of the final one, no further effort is made to resolve it.

Whoever, having thus abandoned that aforementioned Brahman characterized by excellence and deficiency, knows "I am non-dual, truth, consciousness, and infinite"—he is one who knows thus (*evaṃvit*). This is because the word *evam* (thus) serves to refer back to what has been previously mentioned.

What is that? Having departed from this world—this world being indeed a collection of perceived and unperceived desirable objects—he, having departed from this world and turned back, becoming indifferent, enters this self consisting of food as previously explained; he does not perceive the multitude of objects as distinct from the body-self consisting of food, but rather perceives everything that has become gross as the self consisting of food; such is the meaning.

Then, from within this *prāṇamaya* which resides undivided within the self of the *annamaya*, he approaches this *manomaya*, this *vijñānamaya*, and this *ānandamaya* self; then he finds fearless support in that which is invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and without abode (TaittU 2.7.1). Regarding this, the following must be considered: who is this "knower" (*evaṃvit*) and how does he transition? Is the agent of the transition someone other than the supreme self, distinct from it, or is it that very self?

What follows from this? If it were something else, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti texts: "Having created that, he entered into that very thing" (TaittU 2.6.1); "He who thinks 'he is one and I am another' does not know" (BĀU 1.4.10); "One only, without a second" (ChU 6.2.1); "That thou art" (ChU 6.8.7; 6.9.4; 6.10.3; 6.11.3; 6.12.3; 6.13.3; 6.14.3; 6.15.3; 6.16.3). Furthermore, if it were the case that "he himself attains the self consisting of bliss," the relationship between object and agent would be untenable.

Furthermore, either the state of being in saṃsāra belongs to another [self], or there is the non-existence of another. If the fault applies in both ways and cannot be avoided, then this inquiry is useless. Alternatively, if the fault does not apply in either one of the two positions, or if a third position is faultless, then that alone is the meaning of the scripture, and thus the inquiry is likewise useless. No; for it is for the purpose of determining that [truth].

It is true that once a fault has been established, it cannot be avoided; however, if one of the two [positions] or a third position were determined to be faultless, this inquiry would be useless. But since that has not been determined, this inquiry is indeed purposeful, because its aim is to determine that very point. It is true that the inquiry is purposeful, as it aims at determining the meaning of the treatise. You may be inquiring, but you will not reach a final decision—is it then the case that there is no need for a decision? No; rather, it is because there are many opposing views.

"You are a proponent of unity (*ekatvavādī*), for you are one who is devoted to the meaning of the Veda. Indeed, there are many proponents of diversity (*nānātvavādinaḥ*) who are outside the Veda; as such, they are not my adversaries, and therefore you will not resolve my doubt. This alone is my blessing—that you speak of me, a single yogi, as having many yogis as adversaries. Therefore, I shall conquer them all and I shall undertake this reflection. But that [unity] itself must be [the goal], because it is that state which is intended to be expressed."

By the knowledge of that [Self], the state of being the Supreme Self is indeed intended here, as in the statement: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. For it is not possible for one thing to attain the state of another. [Objection: But even for him (the knower), the attainment of that state is equally impossible. [Reply: No; because its purpose is the removal of the non-Self created by ignorance. For the attainment of one's own Self which is taught through the knowledge of Brahman has as its purpose the removal of the non-Self—which is superimposed as the Self through ignorance and consists of specific forms such as food and so forth.

How is this meaning understood? From the teaching of knowledge alone (*vidyāmātra*). And the observed effect of knowledge is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*); and that [cessation] is taught here as the means for attaining the Self through knowledge alone. If it is argued that it is like the teaching of the knowledge of the path, [we reply: that teaching of the means consisting of knowledge alone is not a reason for [the Self] being the path itself. Why? Because we observe the teaching of the knowledge of the path in relation to reaching another location. If it is argued that "one does not go to the village itself," [we reply: no, because of the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*).

For in that context, knowledge concerning the village or its objects is not taught; rather, only knowledge concerning the path to reaching it is taught. It is not so here, where knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman concerning other means is taught. If it is argued that the knowledge of Brahman, depending on previously mentioned means such as ritual action, is taught as the means for attaining the Supreme, we say no; because this has already been refuted by the statement beginning with "Because liberation is eternal," and so forth.

And the scripture, stating "Having created that, he entered into that very thing" (TaittU 2.6.1), shows that the effect has that [Brahman] as its self. Furthermore, the attainment of fearlessness and a firm foundation is logically possible; for if one who possesses knowledge sees nothing other than the Self, then it is said, "he finds fearlessness and a firm foundation" (TaittU 2.7.1), because there is no other, distinct cause of fear. Moreover, since any other [cause] is produced by ignorance, its lack of reality is established through the vision [gained] by knowledge.

For that non-existence of a second moon is not perceived by one with clear vision free from cataracts. If you argue that it is not the case that it is not perceived, we say no; because it is not perceived by those who are asleep or in meditative absorption (*samāhita*). If you argue that its non-perception in deep sleep is like that of one distracted by something else, we say no; because there is a total lack of perception [of anything]. If you argue that since other things are perceived during waking and dreaming, [the second moon] must exist, we say no; because waking and dreaming are produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).

The apprehension [of objects] that occurs in waking and dreaming is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is absent when there is knowledge (*vidyā*). If it is argued that non-apprehension in deep sleep is likewise produced by ignorance, we say no; for it is innate. For the true nature (*tattva*) of a substance is changelessness, because it is independent of anything else. Change is not the true nature, because it depends on something else. Indeed, the true nature of a thing does not depend upon causal factors (*kāraka*); rather, it is a particularity (*viśeṣa*) that depends on causal factors, and a particularity is a change. Furthermore, apprehension in waking and dreaming is a particularity.

For that which has a nature not dependent on anything else is its true reality (*tattva*); that which depends on something else is not its true reality, because it does not exist in the absence of that other thing. Therefore, because it is inherent, there is no distinction in deep sleep as there is in the waking and dreaming states. However, for those who hold that God is other than the Self and that the effect is other [than the cause], fear does not cease; for fear has another as its cause, and it is impossible for an existing thing to perish, nor can a non-existing thing come into being.

If it is argued that for another entity which is dependent [on something else], there can be a cause of fear, we say no; for that case is equal [to the one already refuted]. If another cause of fear were to exist by depending on some cause—whether eternal or non-eternal—that is accompanied by factors such as *dharma*, then for that [dependent] entity as well, fear would not cease because it lacks the destruction of its own self (*ātmahāna*). Or, if there were destruction of the self, then since existence and non-existence would mutually transform into one another, there would be a total lack of security everywhere. However, in the view of unity (*ekatva*), there is no fault, because this transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) along with its causes is merely constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).

For the second moon seen by one suffering from ophthalmia (timira) has neither origination nor destruction. If it is argued that ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) possess that same nature [of being unreal], we say no, because they are perceived directly. Discrimination (*viveka*) and non-discrimination (*aviveka*) are perceived as residing within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), just like color and other objects; for a directly perceived color does not have the status of being a property of the seer. Furthermore, ignorance is manifested through its own experience in the form: "I am deluded," or "my consciousness is undiscriminating. Likewise, discrimination is experienced as knowledge.

The wise teach their own knowledge to others, and others likewise comprehend it. Therefore, knowledge and ignorance belong only to the side of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name-and-form are not attributes of the Self (*ātman*). This is because of another scriptural passage: "That which is distinct from these two, name-and-form, and which lies between them—that is Brahman" (ChU 8.14). Furthermore, those two, name-and-form, are merely conceptual constructs—like day and night in relation to the sun—and do not exist in an ultimate sense.

If it is argued that because there is no difference [between the self and Brahman], the status of being both object and agent in the passage, "He approaches this Self consisting of bliss" (TaittU 2.8.5), is untenable, we say: no, because this "approaching" is merely a matter of cognition. A physical transition like that of a leech is not what is taught here; rather, the meaning of the scriptural term "approaching" is simply cognition. If it is objected that a literal transition is indeed heard in the word "he approaches," we reply: no, because such a transition is not observed in the case of the Self consisting of food (*annamaya*).

For neither is a transition from this external world into that which consists of food (annamaya) observed—whether like the movement of a leech or otherwise—nor is there a transition of the self (ātman) by means of the return of the mind-made (manomaya) or the consciousness-made (vijñānamaya) [sheaths] after they have gone outside. If it be argued that this is so, we say no, because of the contradiction of an action upon oneself; for while the context establishes that "one [entity] different from the one consisting of food transitions into another," it would be a contradiction for the mind-made or the consciousness-made to transition into its own very self.

Likewise, the transition of the self into that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya) is not tenable. Therefore, "transition" is neither an attainment, nor is it an action performed by any one of the [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya); rather, by process of elimination, transition is established as a mere act of knowledge performed by an agent distinct from the selves beginning with the one consisting of food and ending with the one consisting of bliss.

If it is pure consciousness alone, then for that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), which dwells within all and is the innermost of all, having created the effects beginning with space and ending with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), and having entered them, there arises the delusion of self regarding the non-self—such as the one consisting of food—due to its connection with the cave of the heart. This delusion perishes through the transition (*saṅkramaṇa*) by means of the arising of discriminative knowledge of the Self. It is in this destruction of the delusion of ignorance that the word "transition" is used figuratively; for otherwise, a transition of the omnipresent Self is not possible, and because there is no other entity [into which it could move].

Nor is there a transition of the self into itself; for a leech does not transition into its own self. Therefore, for the sake of realizing the Self characterized as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," such things as becoming many, entering creation, obtaining the essence, fearlessness, and transition are merely conceptualized in Brahman—which is beyond the scope of all empirical discourse—but in the ultimate sense, no conceptual construction whatsoever is possible in the non-conceptual Brahman.

Having approached this very self, which is free from conceptual construction, in this sequence and having known it, one does not fear anything; one finds the foundation of fearlessness (*abhaya*). With regard to this meaning, there is also this verse. This mantra serves to briefly illuminate the entire subject matter of this section, the *Ānandavallī*. Thus ends the eighth section (*anuvāka*).

"From whence words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—having known that bliss which is Brahman, one fears nothing at all. Indeed, this does not afflict him: "Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is evil? He who knows thus protects these two by means of the Self; for he who knows thus protects both by means of the Self. This is the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the ninth section.
Thus ends the Brahmavallī.

Because, from that non-conceptual Self characterized as described above—the non-dual bliss—verbal expressions (*vācaḥ*), which have as their objects things possessing conceptual distinctions such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, are employed by speakers for the purpose of illumination even with respect to Brahman, which is non-conceptual and non-dual; yet, failing to reach it and failing to illuminate it, they turn back and fall away due to their own inherent incapacity. The term "mind" (*manaḥ*) refers to the cognition (*vijñāna*).

And wherever that designation has been applied, it functions to illuminate even an object beyond the senses; and wherever there is cognition, there is the activity of speech. Therefore, in all cases, the activity of both designation and cognition proceeds simultaneously with speech and mind.

Therefore, since even words employed in every possible way by speakers to reveal Brahman turn back—along with the mind and the consciousness capable of illuminating everything—from that which is beyond the scope of cognition, inexpressible, and characterized by such attributes as being invisible and so forth; [one realizes] that bliss of Brahman, which is the very self of the Vedic scholar who is free from crookedness and untouched by desire, who is liberated from all longings, and whose bliss is natural, eternal, indivisible, and free from the relationship between object and subject.

One who knows the Brahman as supreme bliss, according to the method described, does not fear anything from any source. This is because of the absence of a cause for fear; for there exists no other distinct object separate from that Knower from which he might fear. It is logical [to say] that fear arises for one who creates a separation within himself through ignorance (*avidyā*). However, for the Knower, since the effects of ignorance have perished—just like the second moon seen by one with a cataract—it is appropriate to say that he "does not fear anything. Thus, because the cause of fear has been destroyed, it is fitting that he fears nothing.

The mantra cited as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) is so called because the mind is the means for the realization of Brahman. In that context, having superimposed the nature of Brahman [upon the mind], the mere absence of fear is enjoined for the purpose of its praise by the words "he fears nothing at any time. Here, however, in the context of non-duality (*advaita*), the very cause of fear is prohibited by the words "he fears nothing from anywhere."

"Is it not the case that there is a cause for fear in the non-performance of good deeds and the performance of evil? It is not so. How is this said?—This [Self], being of such a nature as described, 'ha vāva' (indeed, certainly) does not burn, does not agitate, and does not torment. But how is it said that the non-performance of good and the performance of evil do not torment? Why? Because at the time when death is near, one experiences remorse, thinking: 'Why did I not perform, why did I not do what is good and beautiful?'"

Likewise, there arises the torment [of remorse] from the fear of suffering such as falling into hell, thinking, "Why have I committed this forbidden act? Why have I done this sin? These two—the failure to perform what is good and the performance of what is evil—do not torment him in the same way that they torment the ignorant man.

Why, then, do they not afflict the wise person? It is said: he who knows thus protects—that is, delights or strengthens—himself by realizing that these two, the good and the evil, are the causes of affliction; the meaning is that he perceives both through the nature of the Supreme Self. For since this wise one has thus made both merit and demerit empty of their own specific forms by regarding them as the very form of the Self, he indeed protects himself.

Who? He who knows thus—that is, he who knows Brahman as non-dual bliss as described—for him, merit and demerit, when seen as his own self-nature, become powerless and no longer cause torment by initiating future births. This is the meaning: that this very Upaniṣad of the knowledge of Brahman, as presented in this Vallī, has revealed the supreme secret among all sciences; for the highest good is seated within it.
The Bhṛgu Vally Upanishad. Om! May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor; may our study be illumined; may we not hate each other. Om! Peace! Peace! Peace!

"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (TaittU 2.1.1). Having created the effects beginning with space and ending with that which consists of food, it has entered into them; because it is perceived as if possessing particularity, one should know that very Brahman—which is distinct from all effects and characterized by attributes such as being invisible—to be bliss itself, thinking "I am That," for the purpose of its entry was precisely that.

For one who understands in this way, auspicious and inauspicious karmas do not become the initiators of another birth; such is the meaning intended to be expressed in the *Ānandavallī*. And thus, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is completed. Hereafter, austerity (*tapas*), which is the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman, must be stated, as well as the meditations (*upāsanā*) concerning food and other subjects that have not yet been mentioned; therefore, this [section] is commenced.

Bhṛgu Vāruṇi indeed approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Venerable sir, teach me Brahman. He spoke this to him: "Food, breath, eye, ear, mind, and speech. He said to him: "That from which these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at their passing—that you must seek to understand; that is Brahman. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he [realized it].
Thus ends the first section (anuvāka). // 1 //

The narrative is for the purpose of praising knowledge; it was spoken by a father to his dear son, as in the case of "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa. The word *vai* serves to recall what is well-known; the one well-known by the name Bhṛgu is thus recalled. "Vāruṇi" means the offspring of Varuṇa; as the son of Varuṇa, desiring to know Brahman, he approached his father Varuṇa with this mantra: "Teach me, O Blessed One, Brahman!"—that is, "Instruct me, explain it to me."

And that father, having spoken these words to his son who had approached him according to the prescribed rule—namely, "Food, life-breath, sight, hearing, mind, and speech"—explained that food is the body, and life-breath is its internal consumer; immediately thereafter, he stated that sight, hearing, mind, and speech are the instruments of perception and the gateways for the realization of Brahman. Having thus described these gateways, food and the rest, he spoke to Bhrigu regarding the defining characteristic of Brahman. What was that?

Since from this [Brahman] these beings, beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass, are born; since, once born, they live by it—meaning they sustain their vital breaths and grow; and at the time of destruction, toward which they go—that is, they return to that Brahman and enter into identity with it, such that during the times of origin, subsistence, and dissolution, the beings do not abandon their nature as that [Brahman]; this is the defining characteristic of Brahman. Therefore, desire to know that Brahman; seek to know it specifically.

The meaning is: "Realize that Brahman which has such characteristics by means of food and so forth. Furthermore, another scriptural passage—*prāṇasya prāṇam uta cakṣuṣaścakṣur uta śrotrasya śrotram annasyānnam manaso ye mano viduste nicikyur brahma purāṇam agrayam* (BĀU 4.4.18)—shows that these are the gateways for the realization of Brahman.

Having heard from his father the gateways for the attainment of Brahman and the definition of Brahman, that Bhṛgu performed austerities (*atapata*) as the means for the attainment of Brahman. But how did Bhṛgu come to understand that austerity is the means, even though it had not been explicitly taught? [The answer is: It was stated with a remainder (*sāvaśeṣokta*). For, regarding the attainment of Brahman through food and so forth, [the father] spoke of the gateway and the definition starting with "from which indeed these... (*yato vā imāni*), and so on. That [instruction] was indeed incomplete because Brahman itself was not directly pointed out.

For otherwise, he should have pointed out Brahman by its very nature to his son who desired to know it, saying, "Brahman is of such-and-such a form. But he did not point it out in this way; rather, he spoke with something remaining unsaid. Therefore, it is understood that the father certainly expects some other means for the realization of Brahman. And the practice of specific austerity is [the means], because it is the most effective of all means.

For it is well known in the world that among all means of accomplishment whose objects are certain to be achieved, austerity (*tapas*) alone is the most effective means. Therefore, although it was not specifically instructed by his father, Bhṛgu undertook austerity as a means for the realization of Brahman. And that austerity consists in the concentration of the external and internal organs, because the realization of Brahman occurs through its medium. Indeed, the one-pointedness of the mind and the senses is the supreme austerity.
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "That which is superior to all dharmas is called the supreme dharma"; and he, having performed that austerity... // 1 //

"Food is Brahman"—thus he understood. "Verily, from food indeed these beings are born; by food, once born, they live; into food they pass and merge. Having realized this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me, venerable sir, Brahman. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity; austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, [he understood].
Thus ends the second section.

"He understood—that is, he realized—'Food is Brahman. For that [food] indeed possesses the characteristics previously described. How so? 'For truly, from food alone these beings are born; by food, once born, they live; into food they enter at death. Therefore, the intention is that it is logical for food to be Brahman. Having thus performed austerity and having realized "Food is Brahman" through both its defining characteristics and logical reasoning, he again fell into doubt and approached his father Varuṇa.

"Teach me, O Blessed One, about Brahman. What, then, is the cause of his doubt? It is said: because he observes that food has an origin. Furthermore, the repeated instruction regarding austerity (*tapas*) is for the purpose of determining it to be the most excellent means. As long as the definition of Brahman—which is unsurpassed—has not been established, and as long as the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) does not cease, austerity alone is your means. The meaning is: "By austerity alone, seek to understand Brahman. The rest is straightforward.

"Life-breath (*prāṇa*) is Brahman," he understood. "Indeed, from life-breath alone these beings are born; by life-breath, once born, they live; into life-breath they enter at their departure. Having understood this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me, venerable sir, Brahman. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity (*tapas*); austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, [he understood]. 1.
Thus ends the third section.

"He understood that the mind is Brahman; for indeed, from the mind alone these beings are born; once born, they live by the mind; at death, they enter back into the mind. Having realized this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, O Venerable One. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity; austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity...
Thus ends the fourth section.

"Consciousness is Brahman," he understood. "Indeed, from consciousness alone these beings are born; by consciousness, once born, they live; into consciousness they enter at death. Having understood this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, venerable sir. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity; austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, he—
Thus ends the fifth section.

"Bliss is Brahman," he understood. Indeed, from bliss alone these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live; into bliss they enter at their passing away. This is that knowledge of Bhārgava and Vāruṇi, established in the highest heaven. He who knows this becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great through offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge; he becomes great in fame.
Thus ends the sixth section.

Thus, having purified his self through austerity, Bṛgu—perceiving the characteristics of Brahman only partially within the vital breaths and other elements—gradually entered further inward and came to know the innermost Brahman as bliss, by means of austerity alone as his instrument. Therefore, the meaning of this section is that one who desires to know Brahman must practice supreme austerity, characterized by the concentration of both the external and internal organs.

Now, having concluded the narrative, the Scripture states in its own words the matter established by that narrative: "This very Vāruṇī knowledge—known by Bhṛgu as the Bhārgavī, taught by Varuṇa—is established and perfected in the supreme non-dual Bliss within the cave of the heart-ether, having proceeded forth from the Self consisting of food."

Whoever else, by this very means of austerity and by this same sequence, enters and knows Brahman as bliss—he, through being established in that knowledge, becomes firmly established in bliss, the supreme Brahman; the meaning is that he becomes Brahman itself. And the visible fruit for him is stated: "Possessing food" (*annavān*) means that abundant food exists for him. For if it were merely a matter of existence, everyone would indeed possess food, and thus there would be no distinction for this knowledge.

The meaning is that by eating thus, one becomes an eater of food and possesses a kindled digestive fire. One becomes great. By what means is this greatness attained? To this he says: by progeny, such as sons and so forth; by cattle, such as cows, horses, and so forth; and by Brahmanic splendor (*brāhmavarcasa*), which is the luster resulting from tranquility, self-control, knowledge, and the like. One becomes great through fame, that is, renown arising from virtuous conduct.

One should not revile food; that is a violation of one's vow. Food is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the body is the eater of food. The body is established in the vital breath, and the vital breath is established in the body. Thus, this food is established in food. He who knows that this food is established in food becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great through offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame.
Thus ends the seventh section.

Furthermore, since Brahman is known through food as its means, one should not revile food as one would a teacher; this is the vow prescribed for such a knower of Brahman. The instruction regarding the vow is for the sake of praising food, and food receives praise because it is the means for the realization of Brahman. Indeed, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is food, because the vital breath exists within the body. Whatever is established within it becomes its food.

And the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established in the body; therefore, the vital breath is food (*anna*) and the body is the eater of food (*annāda*). Likewise, the body is also food and the vital breath is the eater of food. Why is the body established in the vital breath? Because the stability of the body is dependent upon it. Therefore, both of these—the body and the vital breath—are food and the eater of food. That by which they are established in one another is food; that by which they provide mutual support is the eater of food.

Therefore, both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the body are food and the eater of food. He who thus knows this food as established in food becomes established by means of the very self that consists of food and the eater of food; furthermore, he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food, and so forth, as described previously.

One should not reject food; that is a violation of one's vow. Water indeed is food; light is the eater of food. Light is established in water; water is established in light. Thus, this food is established in food. He who knows that this food is established in food becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great through offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame.
Thus ends the eighth section.

"One should not reject food" means one should not avoid it; that vow is for the sake of praise, as before. Thus, food that is not abandoned through the conceptualization of "pure" or "impure" would be praised and magnified. In this same way, one should apply what has been stated to the subsequent cases as well, such as "water, indeed, is food," and so forth.

One should hold food in high esteem; that is the vow. Earth is food; space is the eater of food. Space is established upon the earth; the earth is established upon space. Thus, this food is established upon food. He who knows that this food is established upon food becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great in offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame.
Thus ends the ninth section.
With the mantra "In the waters is light," there is the vow of providing abundant food for the practitioner who meditates upon water and light as possessing the qualities of the eaten and the eater.

One should not refuse anyone seeking lodging; that is his vow. Therefore, by whatever means possible, he should obtain much food. "Food has been prepared for us," they say. This is indeed food prepared at the beginning; for him, food is prepared at the beginning. This is indeed food prepared in the middle; for him, food is prepared in the middle. This is indeed food prepared at the end; for him, food is prepared at the end.

Likewise, for one who worships the earth and space, no one at all should refuse him lodging; the meaning is that he should not turn away anyone who has come for the purpose of a place to stay. And once lodging is given, food must certainly be provided. Therefore, by whatever means and in whatever manner he may obtain abundant food, he should make a store of much food—this is the meaning.

Because learned men who possess food, when approached by one seeking food, declare, "Food has been prepared for you," and do not refuse him by saying, "There is none," for that reason he shall obtain abundant food; this is the connection with what precedes. Furthermore, the greatness of giving food is stated: at whatever time one gives food, at that very same time it returns to him.

To the question "How so?", this is said: "This food, indeed, prepared with honor for one who has arrived seeking food—either 'from the mouth,' meaning in the first stage of life, or 'by the principal means,' meaning by the primary mode of livelihood—he gives. What would be the fruit of that? It is said: "From the mouth," meaning in the earlier stage of life, or by the principal means, food is obtained for this giver of food; the meaning is that it comes to him just as it was given.

In this way, in the middle of life, at the middling time, and with middling treatment; likewise, in the end of life, at the final time, and with inferior treatment and contempt—in that very manner, food is prepared for him and becomes successful.

"Safety" is in speech; "acquisition and preservation" (yogakṣema) is in the out-breath and in-breath; "action" is in the hands; "motion" is in the feet; "liberation" is in the anus—these are the human designations. Now, the divine ones: "satisfaction" is in rain; "strength" is in lightning.

Whoever knows this—meaning whoever knows the greatness of food as described above, as well as the fruit of its giving—the aforementioned fruit accrues to him. Now, the method of meditating upon Brahman is stated: "Security (kṣema) in speech. Security means the protection of what has already been acquired. One should meditate that Brahman is established in speech in the form of security. "Acquisition and security" (yogakṣema): acquisition (yoga) is the obtaining of what has not yet been obtained.

For although those two, acquisition (*yoga*) and preservation (*kṣema*), exist when the *prāṇa* and *apāna* exist, they do not have the *prāṇa* and *apāna* alone as their cause; rather, they have Brahman as their cause. Therefore, Brahman is to be meditated upon as being established in the *prāṇa* and *apāna* by way of acquisition and preservation. In the same way, among the others that follow, Brahman alone is to be meditated upon through this or that particular aspect. Since action is brought about by Brahman, Brahman is to be meditated upon as being established in the hands by way of action. "Gait" [is to be meditated upon] in the feet.

"Liberation" refers to the anus. These are the human designations—that is, those pertaining to humans among men; "designations" means internal cognitions, knowledges, and forms of consciousness, which is to say, objects of worship. Immediately after this, the divine designations—those pertaining to the gods among the gods—are stated. "Satisfaction" refers to rain. Since rain is the cause of satisfaction by way of providing food and other necessities, Brahman itself, established in the form of rain as the essence of satisfaction, is to be worshipped. Likewise, in other things, Brahman alone is to be worshipped in its respective form; similarly, in lightning, it is to be worshipped in the form of power.

"One should meditate on it as fame among cattle; as light among the stars; as procreation, immortality, and bliss in the organ of generation; and as the All in space. By meditating on it as 'the foundation,' one becomes possessed of a foundation. One should meditate on it as 'the great'; one becomes great. One should meditate on it as 'the mind'; one becomes possessed of a mind."

In the form of fame among cattle; in the form of light among the stars; procreation, immortality—the attainment of immortality—and bliss, which is happiness through the son as the means of release from debt: all this, having Brahman as its cause, is established in the organ of generation by means of this Self; thus it is to be meditated upon. For everything is established in space; therefore, that which is everything in space is Brahman alone—thus it is to be meditated upon. And that space is indeed Brahman. Therefore, one should meditate upon it as the support of all.

By meditating upon [Brahman] as "Foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*), one becomes possessed of a foundation. In this same way, regarding the preceding [attributes] as well, it should be understood that whatever fruit is taught in connection with a particular attribute, one becomes possessed of that very fruit by meditating upon Brahman as such. This is also known from another scriptural passage: "In whatever way they meditate upon Him, that very thing they become" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.5.2.20). One should meditate upon It as "Greatness" (*mahaḥ*). One should meditate upon It as possessing the quality of greatness; [thereby] one becomes great. One should meditate upon It as "Mind" (*manas*). "Mind" (*manas*) is the act of thinking (*manana*); [thereby] one becomes possessed of mind, that is, one becomes capable of reflection.

One should meditate upon it as "the Name" (*nāman*); desires bow down to him. One should meditate upon it as "Brahman"; he becomes possessed of Brahman. One should meditate upon it as "the complete death of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ parimara*); those who hate him, his rivals, and those enemies who are unpleasant to him, die around him. That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun are one.

One should meditate upon it as "the Name. "Namo" means bowing; one should meditate upon it as possessing the quality of being bowed to. Desires—meaning objects of enjoyment that are desired—bow down, become humble, before this meditator. One should meditate upon that as Brahman. One should meditate upon it as the most preeminent Brahman. One becomes possessed of Brahman, endowed with its qualities. One should meditate upon that as the complete absorption of Brahman.

The "complete dying around" (*parimara*) of Brahman is that in which five deities—namely lightning, rain, the moon, the sun, and fire—die away. Therefore, Vāyu is the *parimara*, as established by another scriptural passage. Since this very Vāyu is non-different from space (*ākāśa*), space is the *parimara* of Brahman; therefore, one should meditate upon space, whose essence is Vāyu, as the *parimara* of Brahman.

Those who rival this one who knows thus—whether they be hateful enemies or even those who are not hateful—are distinguished as "hateful rivals" (*dviṣantaḥ sapatnāḥ*) because they exist as such. Those hateful rivals perish around him; they abandon their vital breaths. Furthermore, those who are his unpleasant kinsmen (*bhrātṛvya*), even if they are not hateful, they too perish around him. Starting from the statement that "breath is indeed food and the body is the eater of food," the relationship of food and eater has been explained for the entire range of effects ending with space.

Granted that it has been stated; what of it? By this, the following is established: transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which is characterized by the state of being the eater and the eaten, pertains only to the realm of effects (*kārya*), and not to the Self (*ātman*). Rather, it is figuratively attributed to the Self through delusion. [Objection: But surely the individual self (*ātman*) is also an effect of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); therefore, transmigratory existence is logically applicable to it. [Reply: No, because of the scriptural teaching regarding the entry [of the Self] into that which is itself non-transmigratory.

"Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (TaittU 2.6.1). For thus the scripture declares the entry of the Supreme Self—who is not subject to transmigratory existence—into His effects, as He is the cause of ether and the rest. Therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) who has entered into the effect is none other than the Supreme Self, which is not subject to transmigratory existence. Furthermore, this is established by the grammatical propriety of a single agent for the two actions: "having created" and "entered. If there were one and the same agent for the acts of creation and entry, then the suffix *-ktvā* is appropriate. If it is argued that for one who has entered, there must be the attainment of a different state of being, we say: no.

Because entry [into the body] has already been rejected on the grounds that it serves another purpose; for if it is argued that there is entry by way of some other attribute due to the specific scriptural statement, "By this living soul" (ChU 6.3.2), we say no, because its identity with That is subsequently stated in "That thou art" (ChU 6.8.7; 6.9.4; 6.10.3; 6.11.3; 6.12.3; 6.13.3; 6.14.3; 6.15.3; 6.16.3). If it is argued that this is a meditative identification (*sampad*) intended to negate that state for one who has indeed undergone a change of state, we say no, because it is stated: "That is the Truth, that is the Self, that thou art" (ChU 6.8.7; 6.9.4).

[This is known] because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [in passages such as] 6.10.3; 6.11.3; 6.12.3; 6.13.3; 6.14.3; 6.15.3; and 6.16.3). If it is argued that the transmigratory state of the individual soul (*jīva*) is observed, we say no; for the perceiver cannot itself be perceived. If it is argued that the Self is perceived as qualified by the attributes of transmigratory existence, we say no; for since attributes are not distinct from the substrate (*dharmin*), it is impossible for them to function as objects of cognition. If it is argued that its state of suffering is inferred from the observation of fear and so forth—just as heat and light cannot themselves be burned or illuminated—[we reply: no.

No; because fear and so forth, as well as suffering, are perceived, they cannot be attributes of the perceiver. If it is argued that this contradicts the systems of logic such as those of the followers of Kapila and Kaṇāda, we say no; for those systems are established as erroneous due to their lack of a valid foundation and their contradiction with the Veda. Furthermore, the non-transmigratory nature of the Self is established by both scripture and reasoning, as well as by its oneness. How is there oneness? It is stated: "That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun, these are one," and so forth, as explained previously in full.

He who knows this, having departed from this world, having approached this self consisting of food, having approached this self consisting of vital breath, having approached this self consisting of mind, having approached this self consisting of consciousness, having approached this self consisting of bliss, wandering through these worlds, assuming at will whatever forms he desires, sits singing this *sāman*: "Hā3vu! Hā3vu! Hā3vu!"

Having approached the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) by way of the sequence beginning with the Self consisting of food (*annamaya*), he remains singing that *sāman*. The meaning of the verse "Truth, Knowledge" has been explained in detail by the *Ānandavallī*, which serves as its commentary. However, the expansion of the meaning of its statement regarding the fruit—"He enjoys all desires together with the omniscient Brahman"—has not yet been stated.

"What are these desires? What is their object? Or how does one enjoy them together with Brahman?"—this must be explained, and so this [section] is now commenced. In that regard, within the narrative of the father and son which serves as a supplement to the preceding knowledge, austerity has been stated to be the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman; the application of all effects, from the vital breaths up to ether, by way of food and the eater of food has also been stated; and meditations (upāsanās) concerning Brahman have likewise been taught.

Furthermore, all desires have been shown to be accomplished by various specific means and to have as their objects distinct effects such as space and so forth. However, if [Brahman] were a single unity, the fulfillment of desires according to one's wish would be impossible, because everything born of differentiation would be identical with its own Self. In that case, how is it said that "one who knows thus enjoys all desires simultaneously through the nature of Brahman"? It is because of the logical possibility of being the Self of all.

To explain how the realization of being the self of all is established, he says: by means of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self residing in the Sun and the Person, one discards the notions of superiority and inferiority; having successively passed through the stages beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*)—which are superimpositions of ignorance upon the Self—and ending with the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), one attains the fruit that is the ultimate result: Brahman, which is truth, knowledge, and infinite, characterized by attributes such as being invisible, and which is natural bliss, unborn, immortal, fearless, non-dual, and free from the world of names and forms. The connection with the distant phrase is: "wandering through these worlds, beginning with the earth. How does one wander?

"Kāmātrī" means one for whom food comes by desire; likewise, "kāmarūpī" means one who assumes forms at will. Wandering through these worlds with his whole self, experiencing them as his own self, he remains seated singing this *sāman*. Because of its equality, Brahman itself is the *sāman*; singing—that is, sounding—it proclaims the oneness of the Self, which is non-different from all things, for the sake of favoring the world. And singing the fruit of that knowledge, which is the state of having fulfilled all purposes (*kṛtārthatva*), he remains seated. How? "Hā āvu, hā āvu, hā āvu."
The word "aho" is used here in this sense to express extreme amazement. // 5 //

I am food, I am food, I am food. I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food. I am the maker of fame, I am the maker of fame, I am the maker of fame. I am the first-born of the Eternal Law (*ṛta*), prior even to the gods, at the navel of immortality. He who gives me to another, he indeed shall lack [me]. I eat the food that eats the food. I have overcome the entire world. The light of heaven! He who knows thus—this is the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the tenth Anuvāka. Thus ends the Bhṛguvallī. Thus ends the Taittirīyopaniṣad.

What, then, is this wonder? It is said: although the Self is non-dual and stainless, I am indeed both the food and the eater of food. Furthermore, I alone am the maker of the *śloka*. A *śloka* is the aggregate of food and the eater of food; its maker is the conscious one. Or rather, I have fashioned this aggregate of food—which exists for the sake of another (the eater) and consists of many parts—on the grounds that it serves the purpose of another. The triple repetition is for the purpose of manifesting the nature of the wonder. "I am" means "I exist."

The "first-born" (*prathamaja*) is one born first, arisen at the beginning. Of this world of truth (*ṛta*), consisting of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), he is the "navel of immortality" (*amṛtasya nābhiḥ*)—that is, the center of immortality for living beings, meaning that immortality resides within me. Whoever gives food to those seeking food, bestowing it upon them, speaks through the very essence of food; the meaning is that such a person truly protects me, who am thus imperishable and as I truly am.

Furthermore, as for another person who, when the time has come, eats food without first giving it to those in need, him—this man who eats food—I myself eat as food; that is, I consume him. To this he says: "In that case, I am afraid of liberation, because it involves becoming the Self of all. Let there be only worldly existence (saṃsāra), for even if I am liberated, I would still be food and thus subject to being eaten. [The Teacher replies: "Do not fear such a thing, because the teaching of all desires pertains to the realm of conventional worldly activity."

Having transcended through knowledge this sphere of conventional discourse characterized by the eater and the eaten and so forth—which is produced by ignorance—the wise man attains the state of Brahman. For him, there exists no second thing whatsoever from which he might fear; therefore, one need not fear liberation. If this is so, then why does he say, "I am food, I am the eater"? It is said in reply: this conventional discourse characterized by the eater and the eaten is merely a product of worldly convention (*saṃvyavahāra*); it is not an ultimate reality (*paramārtha-vastu*).

Although he is thus constituted, because that which is characterized by Brahman does not exist apart from Brahman, this is stated for the purpose of praising the state of being Brahman—which is the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman: "I am food, I am food, I am food; I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food," and so forth. Therefore, even the slightest trace of defects such as fear, which are caused by ignorance, does not exist for one who has become Brahman through the destruction of ignorance.

I have transcended, I surpass with my supreme sovereign nature, the entire universe—the "bhuvanam," so called because it is to be resorted to (*bhaj*) by beings such as Brahmā and others, or because beings (*bhūtāni*) exist within it. My light is "suvar"; *suvar* refers to the sun (*āditya*), and the letter *na* is used for the sake of comparison. Like the sun, our light—meaning the radiance—is "once-shining" (*sakṛdvibhātam*).

Thus, this is the supreme knowledge of the Self (paramātma-jñāna) established by the two Vallīs; having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, and having undertaken great austerity like Bhṛgu, he who knows this Upaniṣad as it has been described—his fruit is liberation as previously stated.
Oṃ. May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor; may our study be brilliant; may we not harbor mutual hatred. Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace!

Thus ends the commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the teacher of the wandering mendicants of the highest order (Paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka), who was a disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda.
